Rāmatīrtha
------------------------------------------
The Vedāntasāra of सदानन्द (17th century A. D.) is a well-known primary text-book of Advaita Vedānta, popular among the students of Vedānta. Out of the three Sanskrit commentaries on it available now in print, the Vidvanmanorañjanī of रामतीर्थ is also one. Nothing is known about him except that he was a disciple of Svāmi Kṛṣṇatīrtha and might have lived during the 17th century A. D.
His commentary is simple and lucid.

Rāmacarita-mānasa
(‘the Mānasa lake of राम’s story’)
------------------------------------------
Rāma and कृष्ण are the two eyes of Hindu religion, philosophy, culture and ethos.
Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa and व्यास’s Bhāgavata are the two foundational epics or treatises which have given birth to innumerable literary works, with religio-philosophical import, both in Sanskrit and in the various vernaculars of India (and even in the foreign languages of South-East Asia).
One such work which has occupied almost the same place in the hearts of millions of Hindus of North India, as that of वाल्मीकि, is the Rāmacarita-mānasa (also spelt as ‘Rāmcaritmānas’) of तुलसी-dāsa A.

-1623. Perhaps, it will not be an exaggeration to state that in the Hindi speaking belts of North India, it is equally or even more revered than the work of वाल्मीकि.
Historically speaking, तुलसीदास lived in troubled times. It was, according to him, only the path of भक्ति or devotion, that was simple to understand and easy to follow, that could restore true religion in the hearts of all. Hence, the whole purpose of his work was to lead the common people away from the various misleading paths that were masquerading as true religion and re-establish भक्ति as the supreme spiritual sādhana or discipline.
Since his mouth spoke out of the fulness of the heart, filled to the brim with devotion to God (as राम), and the hand just recorded what his heart dictated, an exquisitely beautiful religio-literary work of eternal value was effortlessly created.
The work is extremely popular due to three major factors: the universal human appeal of his conception of भक्ति; propounding the ethical values and spiritual truths through the popular story of राम; and, the unparalleled poetic genius.
Though based mainly on the Rāmā-yaṇa of वाल्मीकि, तुलसीदास has also drawn heavily from another well-known work, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (See ADHYĀTMA RĀMĀYAṆA.) a work of the 15th century A. D., considered sometimes as a part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. (See BRAHMĀṆḌA PURĀṆA also.)
The other two works from which he seems to have borrowed some incidents are: the Hanūman-nāṭaka (also called Mahānāṭaka) and the Prasanna Rāghava, a drama in seven acts, of जयदेव (12th century A. D.).
The whole work is in the Avadhī dialect of Hindī, using mainly two kinds of metres:
dohā (a couplet of four quarters in which the first and the third have 13 mātrās or syllabic instants; and, the second and the fourth, 11 each).
caupāī (similar to dohā but with 16 mātrās in each quarter).
The dohās (which are of primary importance) are distributed as follows, in the seven kāṇḍas or books, the names of which are identical with those of वाल्मीकि’s (except the sixth which is known as Laṅkākāṇḍa instead of Yuddhakāṇḍa):
Bālakāṇḍa (361);
Ayodhyākāṇḍa (326);
Araṇyakāṇḍa (46);
Kiṣkindhā-kāṇḍa (30);
Sundarakāṇḍa (60);
Laṅkākāṇḍa (121);
Uttarakāṇḍa (130).
Each dohā is followed by several caupāīs, the total number of which exceeds five thousand.
Though तुलसीदास has closely followed the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, he has also wrought many changes. In fact, the first part of the Bālakāṇḍa has several such changes and innovations. A few of these may be mentioned here: incidents in राम’s childhood resembling those of कृष्ण given in the Bhāgavata; राम and सीता seeing each other in the garden of मिथिला and being mutually attracted; the breaking of the bow of शिव in स्वयṁवर, before a large assembly of kings; arrival of परशुराम there, immediately after the breaking of the bow, and his subjugation by राम.
Apart from these, other interpolations in the same kāṇḍa are: long introductory passages including prayers, dialogues between the sages याज्ञवल्क्य and भरद्वाज, a long discourse on the story of शिव, dialogue between शिव and पार्वती and the stories of विष्णु’s earlier incarnations.
Some more variations may also be noted.
They are: glorification of भरत as a great devotee of राम; disappearance of सीता into the fire before the arrival of the illusory deer (māyāmṛga) and a shadow सीता (or Māyāsītā) emerging out of it (who will be abducted by रावण, the king of demons); meeting of हनुमान् and विभीषण after the former’s arrival at लङ्का and the latter’s help in locating सीता; advices given by मण्डोदरी, कुम्भकर्ण and Mālyavān to रावण since they had recognised राम as विष्णु himself; and, the conversation between रावण and अङ्गद as well as the one between त्रिजटा and सीता.
It is interesting to note that the Uttarakāṇḍa of Rāmacaritamānasa has two parts, the first part giving a description of राम’s चोरोनतिओन् and that of his rule (Rāmarājya); and, the second part describing the evils of कलियुग as also the need for dāsyabhakti (devotion to God like that of a servant towards his master) which alone can lead to salvation. This second part is in the form of a dialogue between the great crow Kākabhuśuṇḍi and गरुड the eagle-devotee and servant of Lord विष्णु.
Scholars of Rāmacaritamānasa sometimes discover three layers or three stages of development in the work, which is not very important from the standpoint of the devotee who is interested only in drawing inspiration for his life.
Tulasīdāsa was an eminent teacher and propagator of the cult of भक्ति or devotion to God. He utilised राम’s story as a very effective means of spreading it. His cult of भक्ति as reflected in this immortal work has certain special features. They are: insistence on moral conduct which is the prerequisite for practising भक्ति; easy availability of the way of devotion (to God) to all, irrespective of their caste or status in the society; emphasising the need for serving the society as per one’s capacity and not looking upon the life of the wandering मोन्क्स् with any admiration or favour.
Though तुलसीदास sometimes gives allegorical meanings also in his story of राम, there is no doubt as to where his heart really lies!—Brahman the Absolute comes down in the human form of राम, out of infinite compassion to save mankind!
By any standards, this magnum opus of तुलसीदास can hold its head high in the class of literary epics of the world, whether ancient or modern.
See also RĀMĀYAṆA and TULASĪDĀSA.

Rāmānanda
(14th century A. D.)
------------------------------------------
One of the more well-known saints of the Middle Ages, रामानन्द might have lived sometime during the period A.

-1470.
He was born at प्रयाग (Allahabad), his parents being Puyāsadana and Suśīlā. Well-educated in Sanskrit and the Hindu scriptures, he received monastic orders from Rāghavānanda, a saṁnyāsin (monk) of the श्रीवैष्णव tradition of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137). Though devoted to the Rāmānuja tradition and its Viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy, he was much more liberal in his attitude and dealings. He lived mostly in काशी.
It was he who spread the cult of Rāmabhakti or devotion to राम, in preference to that of कृष्ण, mostly in North India.
According to some versions of his life, he migrated from South India where he lived earlier, to the North.
Rāmānuja’s Śrībhāṣya (commentary on the Brahmasūtras) and a less known work, the Agastyasutīkṣṇa-saṁvāda, were his favourite treatises.
He considered राम as same as the ब्रह्मन् of the उपनिषद्स् and the repeti-tion of the Rāmamantra as the best means of लिबेरतिओन्. Instead of the well-known अष्टाक्षरी मन्त्र (Oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya) he adopted the Rāmamantra (given perhaps by his गुरु), rāṁ rāmāya namaḥ as the chief esoteric formula of spiritual life.
Tradition states that he accepted his disciples irrespective of their caste and social status. Among them कबीर् (a Muslim), रैदास् (a shoemaker), Senā (a barber) and पद्मावती (a woman) were well-known, though doubts are expressed by some scholars about the inclusion of some of these names.
The Granth Sāhib contains one Hindi song of his, though that song has not been found in the collection of his disciples.

Rāmeśvaram
------------------------------------------
Pilgrimage to holy places is an integral part of हिन्दुइस्म् in practice. A devout Hindu undertakes the पिल्ग्रिमगे not only because it is a commandment of the scriptures, but also to purify himself and earn पुण्य (religious merit).
Rāmeśvaram has been one of the four most important pilgrim centres—the other three being बदरीनाथ, द्वारका and पुरी or Jagannātha Purī—as also one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् (See JYOTIRLIṄGAS.) which every Hindu used to aspire after visiting, at least once in his lifetime.
The place gets its importance solely due to the legend that Śrī राम, while returning from लङ्का, along with सीता and लक्ष्मण, established a शिवलिङ्ग here and personally worshipped it. (See RĀMALIṄGA for details.)
The town of रामेश्वरम् is situated on a small island which is in the shape of a शङ्ख (conch), 55 kms. (34 miles) by 12 kms. (7 1/2 miles), between the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar. It is connected with the main land (the small town of Maṇḍapam) by a railway and a road bridge, one kilometer long.
The major attraction of this place is the famous temple of Rāmanātha (or Rāmanāthasvāmin), the शिव temple founded by Śrī राम himself.
The present structure, which is of massive proportions, has taken several centuries to take this shape. Even a king of Sri Lanka, apart from the local kings, is said to have contributed to its growth and development.
Rāmeśvaram Temple TowerThe main temple, situated at a distance of 200 metres (660 feet) from the sea covers an area of about six hectares (15 acres).
The speciality of this temple is its huge outermost corridor, rectangular in shape. Its total length is 1220 metres (3700 feet), the width of the path being 5.7 metres (19 feet) and the average inner height 9 metres (30 feet).
There are about 4000 pillars, each 3.7 metres (12 feet) high. All are located on platforms 1.5 metres (5 feet) in height.
Images and motifs are in the Dravidian style and are extremely beautiful.
The stone slabs used for the roof are 13 metres (42 feet) in length!
Out of the four gopurams (towers), the eastern one rises to a height of 42 metres (138 feet) and the western one, to 26 metres (85 feet). Both are embellished with miniature figures. The other two gopurams are incomplete.
As one enters the temple from the main entrance in the east one comes across a huge नन्दि (the bull-mount of शिव).
रामेश्वरम् Temple">An Interior View of रामेश्वरम् TempleThe principal sanctum contains the main लिङ्ग known as Rāmanātha (Lord of राम). This is supposed to have been prepared by सीता herself.
On its left is the shrine of पार्वती (known as Parvatavardhinī).
Near the main shrine are also located two subsidiary shrines dedicated to Viśvaliṅga (the लिङ्ग brought by हनुमान्) and Viśālākṣī (an aspect of पार्वती).
Behind the Rāmanātha shrine is another small shrine dedicated to विष्णु, known as Setumādhava.
In the campus, there are 24 tīrthas (holy tanks) where the pilgrims are expected to bathe, before visiting the main shrine. The first one, as we enter from the western entrance, is the Mādhava-tīrtha which looks like a small lake. The Setumādhava temple is by its side. Most of the other tīrthas are like small wells from which water has to be drawn, for bathing.
Each of these tīrthas is said to possess some special power to destroy sins or bestow extraordinary benefits here or hereafter.
About 200 metres (650 feet) to the east of the temple, the sea is called Agnitīrtha where the pilgrims bathe before entering the main temple.
The footprints of Śrī राम are enshrined in a small shrine called गन्ध-mādana on a hillock, about 2.5 kms. (1.5 miles) to the west of the main temple.
The Kodaṇḍarāma temple, situated at a distance of 8 kms. (5 miles) from रामेश्वरम् towards धनुष्कोटि, contains the images of राम, सीता, लक्ष्मण, हनुमान् and विभीषण. This is said to be the place where विभीषण surrendered to राम.
Dhanuṣkoṭi situated at a distance of 20 kms. (12 miles) to the southwest of रामेश्वरम् is another important pilgrim centre. This is the place where Śrī राम, using his धनुस् or bow partly destroyed the bridge he had got built by the monkey army, at the request of विभीषण who did not want his enemies to invade लङ्का in future!
It is actually the confluence of the two seas, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean.
The pilgrims used to perform śrāddhas (obsequial ceremonies) here. During the cyclone of A.

, much of this place was devastated.
A few of the other holy places near Rāmeśvaram—all connected with Śrī Rāma—are:
Darbhaśayanam where Śrī राम observed penance to please god वरुण.
Ādi-जगन्नाथ तेम्प्ले, which the king दशरथ, along with his wives, visited and prayed for worthy sons.
Devī Pattanam on the sea-coast, containing nine stone pillars representing the nine प्लनेत्स् which Śrī राम worshipped for success in his mission.
Jaṭātīrtha where Śrī राम washed his hair to get rid of the sin he might have incurred in the battle at लङ्का.
The chief festivals celebrated at the Rāmanātha temple are: Mahāśivarātri (during February-March); रामलिङ्ग-pratiṣṭhā (the day of establishing the लिङ्ग by Śrī राम, usually for three days in June); and, the Tirukalyāṇam festival (the day of मर्रिअगे of पार्वती and शिव) in July, lasting for seventeen days.
An important, or even unique feature of this temple is its very rich array of diamond and golden jewellery accumulated over the centuries, due to the munificent offerings of the devotees.
In the olden days devout Hindus always cherished a strong desire to visit काशी, bring the गङ्गा water from there, and bathe the Śivalilṅga at रामेश्वरम् with it.

Rāmakṛṣṇa
------------------------------------------
1. Introduction
The ordinary men of this world, sometimes, become so ordinary that extra-ordinary men have to appear here to lift them up to no ordinary heights, if not extraordinary ones. These tall men who walk this earth, may seem to be no different from others at first, but soon grow to superhuman proportions revealing their true nature even as विष्णु (the all-pervading Divinity) appeared first as वामन (the dwarf) and then as त्रिविक्रम (one who occupied all the three worlds).
Rāmakṛṣṇa—also known as ‘Śrī रामकृष्ण परमहṁस’ or just ‘Paramahaṁsa’—belongs to this rare species. His life was religion—in the highest sense—in practice. He lifted up religion from the morass of rituals and dogmas to great mystical heights as effortlessly as Varāha (the Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) the earth. An earnest study of his life—his doings and sayings—can not only inspire us but also elevate us to transcendental levels.
2. The Exodus
It was a misty morning in A.

. The place was the small village called Derepur in Bengal. Khudirām Caṭṭopā-dhyāya, the highly venerated ब्राह्मण of the village, was about to depart from there, for good, along with his wife Candrā-देवी and the two children, Rāmkumār and Rāmeśvar, for another village, Kāmār-pukūr (112 kms. or 70 miles to the north-west of Calcutta [now Kolkata], the metro-polis of Bengal). Since he had dared to disobey the zamindar (land-lord) of the village by refusing to bear false witness, he had incurred his wrath and had been banished.
Khudirām left nonchalantly, loudly chanting ‘Jay Raghuvīr!’ (‘Victory to Lord राम!’), leaving behind the simple village-folk sorrow-stricken.
As soon as he arrived at कामार्पुकूर्, he was received by his old friend and other villagers, with great warmth, love and affection. They quickly provided the whole family all that they needed, for a simple but comfortable life.
It was this Khudirām who had sacrificed everything for the sake of truth, that was chosen by Destiny to be the ड़थेर् of रामकृष्ण, who declared in his later life that truth is the sine qua non of religion, even in this कलियुग or Iron

. The Visions
Khudirām was fond of पिल्ग्रिमगे. In A.
he had gone to रामेश्वरम् all alone by foot, walking more than 2400 kms. (1500 miles). However, it was during his visit to the विष्णु (known as Gadādhara) temple at गया (in Bihār) in A.

that he had a wonderful vision of the Lord informing him of his decision to incarnate in his होउसे as his son! Almost at the same time, Candrādevī, while paying her homage to Lord शिव in the temple near her होउसे, had another experience, that of a divine light from the icon in the temple entering into her and making her unconscious. When she regained her चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् she felt as if she was with child.
When Khudirām returned home and learnt of her strange experience, his own conviction about the visitation of the Divine got further confirmed.
The couple started eagerly preparing for the auspicious arrival of the Divine Being in their womb through prayers and austerities.
By the by, these two experiences of the holy couple affirm the statements in the Hindu scriptures that विष्णु and शिव are two aspects of the same Supreme

. Nativity and Early Life
The advent of the divine child took place on the 18th February 1836 at about 5:15 A.M.
He was named ‘Gadādhar’ since he was born as the earthly manifestation of the deity Gadādhara-विष्णु of गया.
The infant Gadādhar proved his divinity in various ways by vouchsafing mysterious experiences to the members of the household, especially to his मोथेर् Candrādevī.
As he grew up into an extremely charming and highly talented boy, he became the darling of the whole village. Apart from being healthy and handsome, his extraordinary skills in fine-arts, मुसिच् and acting made him the cynosure of all eyes.
As for formal एदुचतिओन् at the village school, he evinced little interest and specially abhorred mathematics.
Even as a young boy, Gadādhar could get into moods of religious ecstasy as naturally as a bird takes to flying. The first experience of ecstasy came to him as he was walking on the ridge of a paddy field, observing the flight of white cranes against the background of black clouds of the rainy season. The second experience occurred when he was visiting the shrine of the village goddess Viśālākṣī of the nearby Ānūr, in the company of elderly women-devotees. The third happened when he was dressed as शिव on a शिवरात्रि day and brought to the stage for a whole-night drama.
It was sometime during this period that Khudirām passed away and the young Gadādhar experienced the first bereavement of his life. This shock made him realise the transient nature of life here and slowly heralded the dawn of spiritual quest, the quest for the Eternal. The approaching उपनयन ceremony (the ceremony of investiture with the sacred thread, an insignia of brāhmaṇahood) provided him with an excellent opportunity for starting on this quest.
The pure in heart shall see God. Even if they cannot do so immediately, they can at least intuit the divine presence. This is exactly what Dhanī, the servant-maid and Śrīnivās, the bangle-seller did. Both of them had instinctively felt Gadādhar’s immanent divinity.
Dhanī had taken a promise from Gadādhar that he would accept the first alms form her hands during his उपनयन ceremony.
This he did, in spite of vehement opposition from the orthodox brothers; because, for him, truth and keeping up one’s word were the most essential part of religion.
Śrīnivās too had his cup of ambrosia filled up, when one day, he seized the opportunity of ritualistic worship to Gadādhar privately, shedding tears of joy all the while.
5. From the Pond to the Ocean
After the death of his ड़थेर् Khudi-rām, Rāmkumār, the eldest brother of Gadādhar, migrated to Calcutta and opened a ṭol (a pāṭhaśālā, a school of Sanskrit and traditional learning) there, to better his worldly prospects.
When he visited कामार्पुकूर् once (in A.

) he discovered to his dismay that Gadādhar (now a youth of 16) was completely neglecting his studies and spending much of his time in worship and other spiritual pursuits. So, he decided to take him away to Calcutta, not only to educate him but also to get assistance from him in his own profession.
Gadādhar was really sorry to leave his dear village and its simple folk. He must have, at first, felt lost like a small fish shifted from a little pond to a limitless ocean. However, he being like the fish of the मत्स्यावतार (the Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु) that gradually grew to mighty proportions, needed this change for the good of the world.
Rāmkumār, at first, handed over the responsibility to Gadādhar, of conducting ritualistic worship in some houses, which he himself was doing, so as to pay greater attention to his school. Though Gadādhar did this work most willingly and enthusiastically, earning the encomiums of the enchanted householders, he continued to remain as indifferent and impervious as before, towards formal secular एदुचतिओन्.
Rāmakṛṣṇa6. The Encounter
Being the chief-guardian responsible for his future life, Rāmkumār could no longer ignore this. Hence he called Gadādhar one day and admonished him for this negligence of formal एदुचतिओन्.
Gadādhar was neither dull nor immature. His uncanny intellect and mature मिन्द् had revealed to him how the whole world was immersed in ‘kāminī-kāñcana’ (lust and greed), a term which he often used in his later life as a world-teacher, and not in the least in God, the final (and the real) goal of life. So, he had no other go than politely but firmly refusing to fall in line, by declaring that he was least interested in bread-winning एदुचतिओन्.
Himself being a spiritually inclined and refined person, Rāmkumār could understand the aspirations of his younger brother and hence gave him full freedom to chart out his own course of life.
Thus ended the encounter, the first and the last, in their lives.
7. The Stage Divine
When Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi (A.

-1861) the intrepid land-lady of Jānbazār in Calcutta decided to go on a पिल्ग्रिमगे to काशी (Vārāṇasī, the famous पिल्ग्रिमगे centre in Uttar Pradesh) she was commanded by Kālī, the Divine मोथेर्, in a dream, to cancel the पिल्ग्रिमगे and build a temple complex for her at the place (called Dakṣiṇeśvar now), also indicated by her in the same dream.
The Rāṇī lost no time in fulfilling the wishes of the Divine मोथेर्. However, when the temple-complex was fully ready, no ब्राह्मण priest was prepared to undertake the responsibility of ceremonially consecrating it since it had been built by a śūdra woman, thereby proving that man can dispose even when God proposes!
However, God, the final disposing authority, would not take it lying down. Strange as it may seem, it came to the lot of Rāmkumār himself (Remember his bitter opposition to Gadādhar’s accepting the first alms from Dhanī, the śūdra woman!) not only to suggest a way out, but also do the consecration ceremony, as well as the regular daily worship in that very temple!
8. The Turbulence and the Tranquillity
Hardly a year after the consecration of the temple complex, death suddenly snatched away Rāmkumār. Though stunned by this sudden development the Rāṇī, along with her highly competent son-in-law, Mathurānāth Biśvās (A.

-1871), managed to prevail upon Gadādhar, by now known as रामकृष्ण रामकृष्ण or Śrī रामकृष्ण.">1, to take up the worship of the मोथेर् Kālī. He reluctantly agreed on the condition that Hṛday—his nephew who had come there seeking a job in the temple complex—be entrusted with the responsibility of taking care of the ornaments and other valuables. This was of course immediately conceded.
Though रामकृष्ण started worshipping the मोथेर् Kālī in the temple in the usual way, observing all the rituals and formalities, very soon a strange but intense desire gripped his heart to know whether the Divine मोथेर् was actually living in that image or whether it was a lifeless statue of stone. This made him undertake severe—even superhuman—austerities for quite a few months. Unable to bear the poor response from the मोथेर् of the Universe, he tried to end his life with the very sword of Kālī kept in the temple. This resulted in an instant revelation of cosmic चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, first as the living presence of मोथेर् Kālī and then as an ocean of bliss, whose surging waves knocked out of him all awareness of the external world. When he came back into his own, he was a totally transformed person, able to perceive clearly the presence of the Divine everywhere and in everything. As he was gliding from the superconscious to the conscious level, the Divine मोथेर् commanded him to be in the bhāvamukha state. Hereafter, the image was no more an image of stone but the intensely living Divine मोथेर् Herself.
The word bhāvamukha, generally translated as the ‘threshold of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्’ is a special technical term used by रामकृष्ण and needs some explanation since it is not found in the earlier religious works.
A person standing on the threshold of the main doorway of a होउसे is absolutely free to move in or move out at will. Even so, a person who has reached the summit of spiritual experience, attaining identity with the Absolute (or ब्रह्मन्), can come down to the plane of relative चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, of names and forms, and even engage himself in activities that are motivated by infinite compassion, for the good of mankind. Any moment, at will, he can also effortlessly raise his मिन्द् to the level of the Absolute, totally oblivious of the world. Even when he is in the relative plane, he continues to be in touch with the Absolute too, since, for him, it is always one state and not two, as we may surmise.
Rāmakṛṣṇa calls such a person as a ‘vijñāni’.
9. Bind Unbound
If strange are the ways of God, stranger still are the ways of the God-intoxicated men. Utterly unable to understand रामकृष्ण’s state of मिन्द्, people started believing that he was out of his मिन्द्. The news soon got wind and reached the ears of Candrādevī and Rameśvar at कामार्पुकूर्. At their earnest entreaties, he returned to कामार्पुकूर्. To everyone’s surprise रामकृष्ण’s behaviour was completely normal! However, not being prepared to take any chances, Candrādevī and Rāmeśvar secretly started searching for a suitable bride, to get him married, thinking that that would ‘cure’ him of all his ‘madness!’
When even their desperate search proved futile, रामकृष्ण himself came to their rescue, asking them to contact Rāmcandra Mukhyopādhyāya of Jayarām-bāṭi (a village very near कामार्पुकूर्) in whose होउसे was a girl ‘specially reserved’ for him! In spite of the apparent barrier—since Sāradā देवी, the girl, was hardly six years old whereas रामकृष्ण was twentythree—the मर्रिअगे was performed, as all other things like the matching of the horoscopes, were perfectly in order.
Just after the मर्रिअगे, when the women of the village were ceremonially circumambulating the couple with lighted torches, the yellow thread tied on the arm of the bridegroom, signifying the matrimonial ties, accidentally caught fire and was reduced to ashes, without scalding him in any way! This mysterious occurrence was actually symbolic of the worldly attachments and attractions associated with the married life, being destroyed even before its beginning.
Thus, the bind was unbound even before it started binding!
Soon after, रामकृष्ण returned to Dakṣiṇeśvar, leaving Sāradā at her ड़थेर्’s होउसे.
10. Expeditions Inward
Though Lord कृष्ण did not need to perform any action to get something pleasant or get rid of something unpleasant—having transcended all duties—yet, he continuously engaged himself in action, to set an example to mankind (vide Bhagavadgītā 3.22). Similarly, though रामकृष्ण had realised the highest Truth through his own efforts, without the assistance of any गुरु (spiritual teacher), lest the ordinary run of mankind also try to do the same and get into trouble, he now started practising sādhanās or spiritual disciplines under the guidance of competent gurus. Thereby, he lent his weight to the age-old tradition of the formal training of a disciple under a qualified teacher. However, instead of the disciple seeking for the teacher, the teachers themselves came to him by the command of the Divine मोथेर्.
The first to arrive was a saṁnyāsinī (nun), योगेश्वरी by name, but more well-known as भैरवी Brāhmaṇī. Not only did she recognise रामकृष्ण as the third disciple she had been commanded in a vision to guide, but also cured him quickly of his strange malady of a burning sensation all over the body, using a simple recipe. Under her expert guidance, राम-कृष्ण successfully practised even the most difficult disciplines prescribed in the तन्त्रस् (scriptural works extolling the Divine मोथेर् and her worship).
Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī was the first to recognise and to declare that रामकृष्ण was an अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of God, even as श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य was. The gathering of the great contemporary paṇḍits including Vaiṣṇavacaraṇ, the best of them, that had been assembled by Mathurānāth at her behest, conceded it. This was practically the first such recognition which was later confirmed by others such as गौरी Paṇḍit, Padmalocan and Nārāyaṇaśāstrī, themselves erudite scholars and genuine sādhakas.
As the mood of devotion inculcated by the tāntrik practices persisted, there arrived at Dakṣiṇeśvar, a Vaiṣṇava ascetic, Jaṭādhārī by name, carrying the image of Rāmlāla or child राम. To him Rāmlāla was ever a living presence. Very soon, रामकृष्ण discovered the secret and befriended Jaṭādhāri whereas Rāmlāla himself befriended रामकृष्ण! After enjoying filial love towards Rāmlāla for quite some time रामकृष्ण’s heart was satiated with वात्सल्यभाव, an important aspect of the practice of devotion. Jaṭādhāri, on his part, started feeling the presence of Lord राम within his own heart and hence left the image with रामकृष्ण at the time of his departure.
Shortly after this रामकृष्ण practised मधुरभाव (bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्), imitating the love of the गोपीस् of वृन्दाबन् towards कृष्ण, which culminated in a vision of राधा (the best of the गोपीस् and dearest to कृष्ण) who entered into his body and disappeared.
The last to arrive was तोतापुरी, the naked Nāgāsaṁnyāsin, of a hefty build and an uncompromising attitude of Advaita Vedānta. When he saw रामकृष्ण and recognised him as a candidate of the highest order eminently fit for सṁन्यास and hence for advaitic practices, he proposed the same.
After getting the approval of the Divine मोथेर्, रामकृष्ण underwent the ceremonies of सṁन्यास and advaita sādhanā. He was able to raise his मिन्द् instantly to the state of the highest nirvikalpasamādhi in which he remained continuously for three days. तोतापुरी was astounded at this feat of his disciple since he himself had taken forty long years to attain it!
Though तोतापुरी had attained a very high state of unitive चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, he never believed in, even disdained, God with names and forms. According to रामकृष्ण, the two were the obverse and the reverse of the same Truth, like water and ice.
This lacuna, तोतापुरी was able to discover and dispel, through a bitter physical ailment deliberately brought about by the Divine मोथेर् of रामकृष्ण. He departed from Dakṣiṇeśvar as a thoroughly chastened and changed person.
After completing all the major modes of sādhanās or spiritual practices in हिन्दुइस्म्, रामकृष्ण turned his attention towards the practice of Islam under the guidance of a Sufi saint. A vision of the Prophet, and later, of Jesus, both of them entering into him and disappearing, gave him the same mystical experience that he had had earlier.
He was thus convinced that the spiritual disciplines prescribed by the various religions of the world, ultimately lead to the same beatific experience, even as all the radii from the various points on the circumference of a circle lead to the same centre.
The equality of all religions taught by him should be understood in this sense, that they all lead to the same experience of beatitude, if practised seriously and sincerely.
After duly completing the expeditions into his inner Self, रामकृष्ण went on an external expedition, to various places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, to oblige his host Mathur-nāth Biśvās, and, perhaps, to sanctify those places, as the Nārada Bhaktisūtras (69) avers.
11. Consort Deified
While रामकृष्ण was sailing over the unchartered and chartered oceans of religious म्य्स्तिचिस्म्, totally oblivious of his wedded wife Sāradādevī, she at Jayrāmbāṭī, was continuously thinking, when the call would come from him to join him at Dakṣiṇeśvar.
When people carried tales to her parents that रामकृष्ण had gone stark mad, she decided to go to him, to be by his side in that hour of crisis and to serve him to the best of her ability.
When she arrived there, she was pleasantly surprised and extremely happy to see him, not only perfectly normal, but also solicitous about her welfare.
Since neither of them was interested in worldly life, but, only, in spiritual companionship, life was smooth. She became his first disciple and started practising sādhanas under his guidance.
Soon after her arrival, one day रामकृष्ण literally worshipped her as मोथेर् Kālī Herself and offered all the fruits of his spiritual endeavours at her feet. It was on the Phalahāriṇī Kālīpūjā day in A.

.
This unique event in the spiritual history of whole mankind signifies two things: total eradication of lust as the end-result; and, that the filial attitude towards all women is the best means of achieving it.
By this wondrous act, रामकृष्ण made her the co-sharer of all his spiritual attainments which automatically became hers too. Also, by invoking the Divine मोथेर् into her and worshipping her, he roused the power of universal motherhood in her. Her later life is a proof of this.
Thus ended the period in राम-कृष्ण’s life, of all sādhanas. He was now fully ready to transmit his spiritual wisdom and power to worthy disciples.
12. The Lotus Blooms
A fully bloomed lotus does not have to invite the bees! They are irresistibly drawn towards it and hence swarm it. So is the case of truly illumined souls, especially if they are living in the society.
The news of a परमहṁस (the ‘Great Swan’, a godman of the highest order) living in the temple campus of Dakṣiṇeśvar, a suburb of Calcutta, spread gradually, first by word of mouth of those who had met him and later by the writings of Keśabcandra Sen (A.

-1884) a pre-eminent leader of the Brahma Samāj which was a vibrant reform movement of those days, who was immensely influenced by him. His writings particularly attracted the youth of Bengal.
Thus started a regular procession of devotees, seekers and admirers, many of whom later became his disciples.
Narendra and Rākhāl, who later on embraced सṁन्यास (monastic life) and established the रामकृष्ण Order, formed the core-group of the younger devotees. Balarām Bose (A.
-1932)—the famous author of that immortal work The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna—Rāmacandra Datta (A.

-1890) were the most important among the householder disciples.
Durgācaraṇ Nāg (A.

-1899) more well-known as ‘Nāgmahāśay’ was another unique personality who combined in himself the highest ideals of both the householder’s and the saṁnyāsin’s lives, that came under the influence of this great teacher.
Among these it was given to Girīś-चन्द्र Ghosh, a rake who had been resurrected from his miserable state, into a devotee of fiery faith by रामकृष्ण, to boldly and openly proclaim that रामकृष्ण was God Himself whose greatness could not be fathomed even by the great sages like वाल्मीकि and व्यास!
13. Drilling the Disciples
Rāmakṛṣṇa knew very well, the main mission of his advent. It was the redemption of mankind in general and to resusci-tate हिन्दुइस्म् in particular.
The various reform movements that had preceded him, had had only a partial effect on the Hindu society. The Ārya Samāj, though it offered stiff resistance to the proselytizing activities of the Semitic religions, completely ignored the entire gamut of the growth of Hindu ethos over several millennia, by laying stress only on the वेदस् and the Vedic rituals. The Brāhmo Movement on the other hand, Christianised हिन्दुइस्म् to such an extent that it appeared more like Christianity—the religion of the then ruling masters—with a veneer of हिन्दुइस्म्. The Theosophical Movement, in spite of its empathy for हिन्दुइस्म्, had in it weird concepts difficult to digest, especially by the intelli-gentsia. Hence, there was an urgent need to resurrect and exhibit the eternal values of the eternal religion, the Sanātana-धर्म. This रामकृष्ण did, not by intellectual research nor by alluring oratory, but by living it every moment of his life. He was amazed to find that the great truths, engendered in the ancient Hindu scriptures like the उपनिषद्स् and the later addenda based on them like the आगमस् and the तन्त्रस्, were still valid, and, worked even now, if only translated seriously and sincerely, into action.
He was convinced that for the rejuvenation of हिन्दुइस्म्, direct spiritual experience through the paths prescribed by it had to be stressed rather than formalism. For this, he needed a band of dedicated young men who would devote their lives not only to realising these truths but also to propagating them.
The young men like Narendra and others were made of just this stuff. Hence रामकृष्ण spared no efforts in training them vigorously and even commanding them to take up this assignment under the leadership of Narendra (the future Vivekānanda), the genius.
Though this training, or rather the drilling, was quite severe, his infinite love and concern for them made it bearable, or even pleasant.
Since he could easily intuit their inner nature, he would give personal and individual instructions best suited to them. As a result, all of them without exception, made tremendous progress in the realm of the spirit.
As regards the householder-disciples, he was much more considerate. Repetition of the divine name imparted to them and surrendering to the chosen deity were the main instructions given to them.
He also eminently succeeded in emotionally binding them to the younger disciples who would later on become मोन्क्स्.
14. The Curtain Downs
Even the basically tough constitution of रामकृष्ण which had withstood the severest and superhuman austerities, started breaking down under the constant strain of talking, singing and dancing for hours on end. Throat cancer was diagnosed in the latter part of A.

and he was shifted to a suitable place in Calcutta for better treatment, first to Śyāmpukūr and later to the Kāśīpur garden होउसे which was a spacious building and had a vast area around it, full of trees and fresh air.
As the illness progressed—in spite of the best medical treatment available—the younger devotees under Narendra’s leadership organised round the clock service. Sāradādevī did the cooking. The householder-devotees defrayed the expenses.
This illness provided रामकृष्ण an opportunity to cement the young disciples into the future monastic Order and the intimate householder-devotees to stand by them affording necessary support for sustenance.
On the first January 1886, he came down from his room, strolled into the garden and blessed the few householder-devotees who had gathered here, liberally vouchsafing various spiritual experiences like a vision of their chosen deities or ecstatic states, just by a touch or a wish. This day is being observed now as the ‘Kalpataru Day’ (the day of रामकृष्ण becoming like the wish-fulfilling tree of हेअवेन् as described in Hindu mythological lore) in all the centres of the रामकृष्ण Order.
That in रामकृष्ण, these devotees were able to actually see their iṣṭadevatās (chosen deities for contemplation) is further proof of his being an इन्चर्नतिओन्.
Sometime during this period, राम-कृष्ण distributed gerua cloths (cloths dyed in ochre colour generally worn by Hindu saṁnyāsins or मोन्क्स्) to the twelve young disciples serving him and made them collect ड़ोओद् by begging in the typical fashion of the traditional Hindu मोन्क्स्. After he himself tasted a little of it, the disciples partook of the same. This, for all practical purposes, was the launching of the रामकृष्ण Order of मोन्क्स्.
Another significant event of this period was the transferring of his spiritual powers by रामकृष्ण to his beloved and chosen disciple Narendra, in the state of समाधि (superconscious state) and declaring that he would achieve great things in his later life.
Though Narendra by now had been convinced about the avatār-hood of राम-कृष्ण, a doubt did creep into his मिन्द् at this time because of this serious illness. As soon as it arose, रामकृष्ण declared in a firm and distinct voice that he who was राम and कृष्ण earlier, was now रामकृष्ण in this body, though not in the sense of Advaita Vedānta which does not accept any distinction between the individual सोउल् and God.
As the D-day was approaching, which he himself had chosen by consulting the almanac, रामकृष्ण gave final and detailed instructions to Narendra to keep the flock (the young disciples) together.
He departed on the night of 16th August 1886 at 1.02 A.M. by clearly uttering the name of मोथेर् Kālī thrice.
The mortal remains were cremated the next day at the Kāśīpur च्रेमतिओन् ground. There now stands a small monument at that place.
15. The Fragrant Candles
The lotus blooms, bees swarm it, drink its honey and disappear by the time it closes its petals.
True, the bees have been satiated by honey. But, they cannot give it to others!
A burning candle can give light and light up another candle; but it cannot emit fragrance.
An incense can give fragrance when burned, but it cannot give light!
How nice and wonderful it would be if there were candles that could give light as also spread an aroma around them!
This is exactly what रामकृष्ण did when he trained his disciples and launched them into the world to start a movement of true religion and spirituality, a movement that would aim at raising a human being from the biological to the psychological level and ultimately to the level of the spirit.
Each one of these disciples who constituted the original रामकृष्ण Order of मोन्क्स् was a light unto himself and to the world. Each one of them was able to spread the रामकृष्ण fragrance in his own way bringing peace and solace to one and all that came to him. The householder disciples of the great Master stood by them like a bulwark.
If today, the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् and the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् have been able to spread रामकृष्ण’s spiritual message all over the world, it is not a little due to these founding fathers and their worthy disciples and successors.
It is also interesting to note here that today, millions of people all over the world have accepted रामकृष्ण as an इन्चर्नतिओन् and are worshipping him as such. There are several instances of his appearing in द्रेअम्स् and visions, consoling and protecting persons—irrespective of their religion and nationality—even though they had not even heard of him!
It will not be out of place here to give a brief account of these direct (saṁnyāsin) disciples—except that of Vivekānanda which needs a more detailed treatment—arranging the names in the English alphabetical order.
Svāmi Abhedānanda (A.

—1939)
Author of several exquisite Sanskrit hymns on रामकृष्ण and Sāradā Devī—the most popular one being ‘prakṛtim paramām’—Svāmi Abhedānanda was a rare combination of several talents like intellectual acumen, devotional fervour and yogic introspection. He was a good speaker and a prolific writer.
Known as Kālīprasād चन्द्र in his premonastic days, he was born on the 2nd October 1866 in Calcutta to enlightened parents, both of whom were deeply devoted to मोथेर् Kālī. Even from his boyhood days, he was inclined towards the study of Sanskrit. As he grew up he was drawn to the study of philosophical works, both Eastern and Western. His desire to become a योगि brought him to रामकृष्ण who immediately recognized him as a disciple of his inner circle. He progressed speedily in the inner life under the guidance of the Master.
After the demise of the Master, Kālī accepted सṁन्यास along with the other disciples and became ‘Svāmi Abhedā-नन्द’. He was given to much study and contemplation during the early days of his monastic life earning for himself the nickname ‘Kālī Tapasvī’.
When Svāmi Vivekānanda wanted a proper assistant to continue the work in the West, he naturally thought of Svāmi Abhedānanda. The latter’s very first discourse on Advaita Vedānta delivered at London was an instant success. He later shifted to New York. He toured and lectured very extensively in the West (both U.S.A. and Europe) for a quarter of a century. His lectures attracted the cream of Western intellects as also earnest seekers of Truth. He returned to India in 1921 and formed a ‘Ramakrishna Vedanta Society’ in Calcutta to carry on his work in his own way. When he gave up the mortal coil on the 8th September 1939, the era of the direct saṁnyāsin disciples of the Master came to an end.
Svāmi Adbhutānanda (d. A.

)
Svāmi Vivekānanda once declared that Lāṭu (the premonastic name of Svāmi Adbhutānanda) was the greatest miracle of रामकृष्ण. If an orphan servant-boy who had absolutely no knowledge of even the alphabets could rise to such a state of sainthood that scholars of great book-learning would sit at his feet and listen spellbound to his words of wisdom, it was nothing short of a miracle that रामकृष्ण brought about. Hence the appropriateness of his name (adbhuta = wonder).
The early life of the Svāmi is shrouded in mystery. Born in a remote village of Bihar, and orphaned at a tender age, the boy was later brought to Calcutta by his uncle. Good fortune favoured him by getting him the job of a servant in the होउसे of Rāmcandra Datta, a great devotee of रामकृष्ण. The holy atmosphere in the होउसे helped unfold his religious temperament. The frequent errands to Dakṣiṇeśvar brought him into close contact with रामकृष्ण who graciously accepted him as a disciple. Later on, as रामकृष्ण felt the need for an attendant, Lāṭu started living with him and serving him. Since the गुरु was all-in-all for him, his service was exceptionally devoted.
After the demise of the Master, Lāṭu embraced monastic life and became ‘Svāmi Adbhutānanda’. Though he lived a mendicant’s life, he seldom moved away from Dakṣiṇeśvar, his holiest place of पिल्ग्रिमगे. Through hard austerity and long bouts of meditation, he was able to live constantly in God.
He lived for an unusually long period of nine years at the होउसे of Balarām Bose, another great devotee of रामकृष्ण. It was during this period that many earnest seekers would meet him and get their doubts resolved.
He spent his last days at वाराणसी where he breathed his last on April 24, 1920.
Svāmi Advaitānanda (A.

—1909)
The darkness of a crisis in life often acts like the twilight before dawn leading to the effulgence of the sun. When Gopāl चन्द्र Ghosh of Sinthi (Calcutta) lost his wife and was heartbroken, that very grief led him to रामकृष्ण, seeking relief. The contact thus established through a crisis ultimately led to glorious spiritual heights.
Gopāldā—as he was endearingly called—was older than even रामकृष्ण. Nevertheless, the attitude of reverence and devotion he cherished towards रामकृष्ण, his गुरु, was unflinching. It was his good luck that made him instrumental in the birth of the future रामकृष्ण Order of मोन्क्स् by gifting a few pieces of ochre-coloured cloths to रामकृष्ण who personally distributed them among Narendra, Rākhāl and others including Gopāl himself, during his last days at Kāśīpur.
Along with Tārak (Svāmi Śivānanda), Gopāldā was the first to join the Barānagore monastery after the departure of the Master from this world. The monastic name given to him was ‘Svāmi Advaitānanda.’ He spent a few years at the monastery, shifted to वाराणसी for about five years and returned to the newly established Maṭh at Ālambazār, and later at Belūr.
His advanced age prevented him from taking active part in the missionary activities of the new organization.
His personal cleanliness, neat and methodical ways of doing any work, had been admired even by रामकृष्ण.
The Svāmi passed away on the 28th December 1909 at the ripe old age of eighty-one.
Svāmi Akhaṇḍānanda (A.

—1937)
‘I do not covet earthly kingdom, or हेअवेन्, or even salvation. The only thing I desire is the removal of the miseries of the afflicted! ’ If these words of प्रह्लाद, the great devotee, could be found truly reflected in anyone’s life, it was in the life of Svāmi Akhaṇḍānanda, the third President of the रामकृष्ण Order. The Svāmī, known as Gaṅgādhar Ghaṭak before ordination into सṁन्यास, was born on the 30th September 1864 in Calcutta. Even in his boyhood-days Gaṅgādhar was deeply religious and orthodox to the point of being dubbed as ‘oldish’ even by रामकृष्ण himself ! As a corrective measure राम-कृष्ण introduced him to Narendranāth (Svāmi Vivekānanda) who was, for all outward appearances, very heterodox, but inside him he had nothing but God. This acquaintance matured into a deep and lifelong friendship between them.
After the demise of the Master, Gaṅgādhar, who took monastic orders and became ‘Svāmi Akhaṇḍānanda,’ led the unfettered life of a wandering monk. For three years he roamed in the हिमालयस् and visited Tibet also three times. Because of his experience in the हिमालयस्, Svāmi Vivekānanda took him as his guide in his sojourn there.
Svāmi Vivekānanda’s burning words to do something for the poor and illiterate masses, inspired Svāmi Akhaṇḍānanda to do some good work for the एदुचतिओन् of poor children both in Khetri and in Udaipur (in Rajasthan). Finally he started an orphanage at the village of Sargacchi in the Murshidabad district of Bengal to where he had gone to conduct famine relief work. He and the institution grew up with each other.
On the death of Svāmi शिवानन्द, स्वामि Akhaṇḍānanda was elected as the third President of the रामकृष्ण Order.
The Svāmi had a flair for learning languages, which brought him into intimate contact with the people wherever he went. His childlike simplicity endeared him to one and all. His austerity and scholarship were a source of inspiration for many.
He breathed his last on February 7, 1937.
Svāmi Brahmānanda (A.

—1922)
Svāmi Brahmānanda, the ‘Spiritual Son’ of रामकृष्ण, was the first President of the रामकृष्ण Order. Known as Rākhāl चन्द्र Ghosh in his premonastic days, he was born at Sikra, a village near Calcutta, on the 21st January 1863, of aristocratic parents. During his highschool days at Calcutta he came into contact with Narendranāth (Svāmi Vivekānanda) which developed into an intimate lifelong friendship. Even from his childhood days he was given to devotional moods bordering on म्य्स्तिचिस्म्, which naturally led to indifference to studies. His ड़थेर् got him married at an early age to ward off the religious pursuits from his मिन्द् and fix him up in the world. Strange to say, this very tie of मर्रिअगे brought him to रामकृष्ण who at once recognized in him his ‘Spiritual Son’ as per the vision vouchsafed to him by the Divine मोथेर्. Thus started a course of spiritual intimacy and intensive training under the loving care of the गुरु, which resulted in several exalted mystic moods and spiritual experi-ences. After the passing away of राम-कृष्ण, Rākhāl, along with Narendra and other brother-disciples, embraced monastic life under the name ‘Svāmi Brahmānanda.’ He spent several years as a wandering monk, visiting places of पिल्ग्रिमगे and practising severe austerities. A little before the return of Svāmi Vivekānanda from the West, he came back to the Barānagore Maṭh and started living there. After his return and establishing the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन्, Svāmi Vivekānanda made over the responsibility of running the organization, to him, remembering that राम-कृष्ण had once remarked that Rākhāl had the capacity to rule a kingdom. His uncanny sense in solving even knotty problems and his spiritual eminence of Himālayan heights took the organization to new levels of glory and development. It was a long stewardship marked by work and worship remarkably blended together. During his tenure as the Head, he also guided many earnest spiritual seekers by taking them under his protection, thus fulfilling Svāmi Vivekānanda’s prophetic remark that he was veritably a spiritual dynamo. He passed away on the 10th April 1922.
Svāmi Nirañjanānanda (d. A.

—1918)
The name ‘Svāmi Premānanda’ given to Bāburām by Svāmi Vivekānanda at the time of accepting the monastic orders, was a true reflection of his basic trait, universal love (prema = love). Born to affluent parents on December 10, 1861, Bāburām completed his early schooling in his village of Ānṭpur (Bengal), came to Calcutta for higher एदुचतिओन् and joined the Metropolitan Institution. There he had the privilege of having Sri ‘M’ (Mahendranāth Gupta), the celebrated author of The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna as his Headmaster and Rākhāl (Svāmi Brahmānanda) as his classmate. It was the latter who was instrumental in taking Bāburām to रामकृष्ण. रामकृष्ण examined Bāburām’s features in his own, rather queer, way and was satisfied about his high spiritual potentialities. Increased contacts with रामकृष्ण intensified Bāburām’s inherent spiritual thirst which had been manifesting itself even from his childhood. After the passing away of रामकृष्ण, Bāburām, along with his brother-disciples like Narendranāth (Svāmi Vivekānanda) embraced the monastic life, becoming ‘Svāmi Premā-नन्द.’ He spent most of his life in the monasteries at Barānagore, Ālambazār and Belūr taking care of worship, internal management and training of the new monastic recruits. His innate motherly love endeared him to one and all. Many a young man was reformed by his golden touch. During his later sojourn in several parts of Bengal, especially in East Bengal (present Bangladesh), he inspired the youth to be useful to the society by voluntary service. Though a man of high spiritual attainments, he was wont to hiding them and was very reticent in giving expression to them. The deadly disease of Kālā Āzār took him away on the 30th July 1918.
Svāmi Rāmakṛṣṇānanda (A.

—1911)
It is said that Svāmi Vivekānanda at the time of सṁन्यास wanted to take the name ‘Rāmakṛṣṇānanda’ for himself, but gave it up in favour of Śaśibhūṣaṇ, who, he thought, deserved it best. And, Śaśi deserved it eminently by dint of his devoted service to रामकृष्ण, especially during his last days. The way he served रामकृष्ण when he was alive and the way he carried on his worship through the relics after his passing away were, to say the least, exemplary.
Born on the 13th July 1863—the same year as Vivekānanda—in an orthodox brāhmin family of the Hoogly district of Bengal, Śaśi got a good एदुचतिओन् and an excellent training during the early years which laid the foundation for a lofty character. His very first visit—along with his cousin Śarat (Svāmi Sāradā-नन्द)—to रामकृष्ण forged strong links with him, whom he accepted as the polestar of his life.
During the last illness of the Master, Śaśi toiled day and night to serve him and to look to his comforts. After his demise, when the relics were gathered and established in the shrine of the maiden monastery at Barānagore, it was Śaśi who took upon himself the responsibility of worshipping it as also take care of his monastic brothers who had been fired by an intense spirit of renunciation. No मोथेर् would have served her children with greater feeling and care than Śaśi cared for them.
At the behest of Svāmi Vivekānanda, Śaśi—now Svāmi Rāmakṛṣṇānanda—came down to Madras (now Chennai) to start a monastery there. By his austere life, devoted service and immense scholarship, he was able to put the monastery on a solid foundation, though he had often to pass through fiery ordeals. It was he who kindled the interest of the people in the then princely State of Mysore, in the teachings of रामकृष्ण and eventually start a Maṭh at Bangalore also.
The Svāmi was a combination of intellectual scholarship of the highest level and devotion of the deepest type. In spite of all his stern external discipline, he possessed a soft and motherly heart.
The hard incessant work he did to consolidate the work of the Maṭh at Madras broke even his massive frame. He left the mortal coil on the 21st August 1911.
Svāmi Sāradānanda (A.

—1927)
While in ecstasy रामकृष्ण’s beha-viour would often be mysterious. One day in such a mood, he sat on the lap of a young man, Śarat चन्द्र by name, and remarked, ‘I was testing how much weight he could bear.’ This Śarat चन्द्र who was later known as ‘Svāmi Sāradānanda’ successfully bore the burden of running the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् and Mission as its (General) Secretary for nearly three decades.
Śarat चन्द्र Cakravarti (b. 23rd December 1865) was born at Calcutta in a rich and orthodox brāhmin family. He and Śaśi, who later became Svāmi Rāmakṛṣṇānanda, were not only cousins and family friends but also studied together at the Metropolitan College of Calcutta.
The first contact of the two cousins with Rāmakṛṣṇa—during October 1883—was a turning point in their lives. Friendship with Narendranāth (Svāmi Vivekā-नन्द) gave a further fillip to their spiritual and monastic aspirations.
Śarat, who was an adept in serving the sick, both by temperament and by experience, was one of the few important disciples of रामकृष्ण who nursed him during his fatal illness. After his passing away, Śarat too joined the select band of monastics under the leadership of Narendra and became ‘Svāmi Sāradā-नन्द.’
Like his other monastic brothers, Svāmi Sāradānanda also spent a few years as an itinerant monk practising severe austerities. However, when Svāmi Vivekā-नन्द called him for continuing his work in the West, Sāradānanda went to London first and later to New York for the same. While he was proving to be a great success in the West, especially due to his spiritual attainments, he was recalled to India in 1898 by Svāmi Vivekānanda to take over the executive responsibility of the Rama-krishna Math and Mission as its (General) Secretary in which capacity he served till his last day.
The way he served Sāradā देवी, the Holy मोथेर्, was a model par excellence for anyone to emulate. In order to build a residence for her at Calcutta which would also होउसे the office of the Udbodhan, the Bengali Monthly of the रामकृष्ण Order, he laboured hard. To repay the debts he had incurred in doing so, he wrote the now monumental Bengali work Śrī राम-कृष्ण Līlāprasaṅga (Sri Ramakrishna, the Great Master).
The Svāmi was as learned as he was spiritual. His courtesy and gentleness were so overwhelming that even the rudest of men would melt into submission. Equani-mity and coolheadedness, even under very trying circumstances, were other remar-kable characteristics of his.
Soon after successfully convening the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् Convention at Belūr Maṭh in 1926, he took ill and shuffled off the mortal coil on the 19th August 1927.
Svāmi Śivānanda (A.

—1934)
Svāmi Śivānanda, the second President of the रामकृष्ण Order, was popularly known as ‘Mahāpuruṣ Mahārāj.’
Born probably in 1854 at Bārāsat of West Bengal, in a respectable and deeply religious family, Tārak—that was his original name—got a good एदुचतिओन्, both secular and spiritual. When he was working in Calcutta in an English firm, he got an opportunity of seeing रामकृष्ण about whom he had already heard. Later, when he met रामकृष्ण at Dakṣiṇeśvar, the latter was pleasantly surprised to learn that he was the son of Rāmkanāi Ghoṣāl, his old acquaintance. Needless to say that Tārak had the full approval of his ड़थेर् for becoming a disciple of रामकृष्ण.
Tārak was the first person to join the monastery at Barānagore after the demise of the Master, and was christened ‘Svāmi Śivānanda’ while receiving the monastic orders. Though Tārak had been married, he had successfully kept up the vow of ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy). This made Svāmi Vivekānanda remark in later days that he was a ‘Mahāpuruṣ.’ This name stuck and he became known as ‘Mahāpuruṣ Mahārāj.’ Like his brother-disciples, he also spent a few years as an itinerant monk. But he had to settle down at the monastery in 1897 after the triumphant return of Svāmi Vivekānanda from the West. For some time he was in Ceylon (Sri Lanka) also, preaching Vedānta at the behest of Svāmi Vivekānanda. He also took a leading part in the first plague relief work of the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् in 1899. It was he who started the आश्रम at वाराणसी.
But the most memorable part of his life was during his stewardship of the Ramakrishna Organizations as the President from 1922 to 1934, when he blessed a large number of people with initiation and brought spiritual solace and comfort to thousands of devotees. He passed away on the 20th February 1934 after a protracted illness which never alienated him from his Lord, whose presence he was constantly aware of. He was one of the finest examples of the fact that the beauty and sublimity of the inner life of a holy man can never be described in words but can only be tangibly felt.
Svāmi Subodhānanda (A.

—1932)
At the behest of Svāmi Vivekānanda, but most reluctantly, Svāmi Subodhā-नन्द rose to speak before a gathering of मोन्क्स् and novices of the Maṭh. And lo! There was an earth-quake! (It was the earthquake of 1897.) It was really an ‘earth-shaking’ speech!
Whether the speech was ‘earth-shaking’ or not, the Svāmi could certainly help even the lowliest in spirits, to shake off his dejection. He was a wonderful combination of compassion, love, childlike simplicity and profound spiritual wisdom.
His premonastic name was Subodh चन्द्र Ghosh. He was born in Calcutta on the 8th November 1867. His parents were deeply religious by nature which automatically left its influence on the son also.
Coming to know of रामकृष्ण through a Bengali book of his teachings, Subodh lost no time in meeting the Saint of Dakṣiṇeśvar. Even during the first two visits, रामकृष्ण guaged the spiritual potential of the boy and put him into a deep meditation by mystic methods.
Subodh joined the Barānagore monastery along with the other disciples of the Master and got the name ‘Svāmi Subodhānanda’ after ordination. Because of his simple and childlike nature, he was endearingly called ‘Khoka Mahārāj’ (khoka = child) by his monastic brothers. After much austerities and itinerant life, the Svāmi settled down to a life of service to the suffering humanity. He was very actively associated with many of the relief works of the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन्. He was extremely liberal in the matter of initiation also, especially towards the weaker sections of the society, whom he tried to help in all possible ways.
The Svāmi passed away on the 2nd December 1932.
Svāmi Triguṇātītānanda (A.

—1914)
The depression brought about by the loss of a gold watch led the young Sāradāprasanna to Dakṣiṇeśvar, seeking peace. Master Mahāśaya, the celebrated author of The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna who was his teacher, led him to his future गुरु. The first visit itself forged strong links between them. Fearing that his religious inclination and frequent visits to the Saint of Dakṣiṇeśvar might ultimately induce him to become a monk, his relatives tried hard to change his मिन्द्, taking recourse to, in the process, religious rites and charms. But nothing worked. And, Sāradāprasanna became ‘Svāmi Triguṇā-tītānanda.’
The Svāmi had a strong constitution and was a dare-devil. During his itinerant days he had often been on the brink of disaster and was miraculously saved. It is said that he once underwent surgery for fistula without anaesthetics.
He never cared for his personal comforts but was ever eager to serve others. The famous relief work he organized at Dinajpur (now in Bangladesh) bears testimony to this.
At the behest of Svāmi विवेकानन्द, स्वामि Triguṇātītānanda started the Udbodhan, the Bengali Monthly of the रामकृष्ण Order, and assiduously built it up.
When Svāmi Turīyānanda returned to India from San Francisco, it was Triguṇātītānanda who was entrusted with the responsibility of organizing the Vedānta work there. It was he who built the first Hindu temple in the West.
The great life came to an abrupt end as a result of a mad man’s act of throwing a bomb. He breathed his last on the 10th January 1914.
Svāmi Turīyānanda (A.

—1922)
A few people there are, who appear to live in this world, but do not really belong here. Svāmi Turīyānanda was one of them. Born in a religious family, of ब्राह्मण parents, on the 3rd January 1863 (just nine days prior to the advent of Svāmi Vivekānanda), Harināth Caṭṭopā-dhyāya—that was his premonastic name—was given to much orthodox observances even in his younger days. An innate desire for लिबेरतिओन् in this very life, kindled by the study of Vedāntic works brought him to रामकृष्ण. The Master through his deep spiritual insight and all-encompassing love, quickly won his heart. Not only that, he soon discovered and destroyed two unhealthy trends in his personality—abhorrence of womankind and excessive reliance on self-effort.
After accepting the monastic robes and vows, Harināth became ‘Svāmi Turīyā-नन्द.’ His orthodox mental make-up made him undertake long and arduous journeys as an itinerant monk, and practise severe austerities as also study of the scriptures. Though he had great love and respect for Svāmi Vivekānanda, he was at first averse to active missionary work. But Svāmījī’s love melted his heart. He accompanied Svāmījī to the United States and worked there for about three years. The Shanti Ashrama in California was practically his च्रेअतिओन्.
After returning to India he spent his days mostly in austerity and in training the younger generation of मोन्क्स्. His burning spirit of renunciation, deep faith in the Divine मोथेर्, and insight into the intricacies of the scriptures left an indelible impression on everyone that came into contact with him. His fortitude and the control he could exercise over his body were astonishing.
He left the body on the 21st July 1922.
Svāmi Vijñānānanda (A.

—1938)
Rāmakṛṣṇa one day challenged a young man to wrestle with him. The tall and hefty youth put him down in no time. And the wonder of wonders, the young man soon felt a power entering from रामकृष्ण’s body into his own, making him completely powerless! That was how Hariprasanna had one of his early encounters with the Master.
Born on the 28th October 1868 in a respectable ब्राह्मण family at Belgharia (Calcutta), Hariprasanna Caṭṭopādhyāya (the pre-monastic name of Svāmi Vijñānā-नन्द) received a good एदुचतिओन् from his parents. He became an engineer and rose to the position of District Engineer in the erstwhile State of United Provinces, before renouncing the world.
From his very first visit, रामकृष्ण spotted him out as one belonging to the inner circle and a future monk. He took particular care to instill in him the ideal of ब्रह्मचर्य or celibacy. His visits to Dakṣiṇeśvar and contact with the Master laid a firm foundation for his spiritual life.
When the Master passed away, Hariprasanna who was still a student at Patna (in Bihar), had a strange vision in which he saw रामकृष्ण as if in flesh and blood, standing before him.
Since he had lost his ड़थेर् early and had to support his मोथेर्, he was obliged to take to government service, but kept in touch with the disciples of the Master, especially Narendranāth (Svāmi Vivekānanda). Later—in A.

, to be more precise—he gave up the world and joined the Maṭh then at Ālambazār, and became ‘Svāmi Vijñānānanda’ after ordination.
Since he was an engineer with good experience in building construction, he was entrusted by Svāmi Vivekānanda himself with the task of building the Maṭh campus as also preparing suitable plans for a memorial temple of रामकृष्ण. So he prepared it in consultation with a noted European architect of Calcutta and Svāmījī approved of the same. Due to the sudden demise of Svāmījī and lack of funds, the project had to wait for a long time to be taken up. It was completed and dedicated by Svāmi Vijñānānanda himself on the 14th of January 1938.
A group of young men in Allahabad had formed themselves into an association called ‘Brahmavādin Club’ with a view to uplifting themselves morally and spiritually. They had done so under the inspiration of a devotee of रामकृष्ण. This devotee had left Allahabad in 1900. As luck would have it, Svāmi Vijñānānanda arrived at Allahabad in the same year as a wandering monk. The young men who were delighted to have a disciple of रामकृष्ण amongst them requested the Svāmi to live in the rented premises of their Club and guide them. The Svāmi agreed and lived there for nearly ten years, spending most of his time in austerity and study. He later on established a permanent branch of the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् at Allahabad in 1910.
The Svāmi was a great scholar, not only in Sanskrit and religio-philosophical works but also in अस्त्रोनोम्य् and अस्त्रोलोग्य्.
He was elected the President of the रामकृष्ण Order in 1937 after the demise of Svāmi Akhaṇḍānanda. He strove hard to complete the construction of the temple of रामकृष्ण at Belūr Maṭh, which he successfully did and dedicated in January 1938 as already indicated. He then retur-ned to Allahabad and passed away on the 25th April the same year. The body was consigned to the sacred waters of the त्रिवेणी, at the confluence of the rivers गङ्गा and यमुना, and the invisible सरस्वती.
Svāmi Yogānanda (A.

—1899)
Though counted among the disciples of रामकृष्ण and guided by him, Svāmi Yogānanda was the first initiated disciple of Sāradā देवी, popularly known as the ‘Holy मोथेर्’. Like the मोथेर् whom he served meticulously with matchless devotion, his life was very unobtrusive for all outward appearances but very deep in inner mystic experiences, of which he sometimes gave a hint or two. Born in 1861 in an orthodox ब्राह्मण family which was in indigent circumstances but had once been aristocratic and rich, Yogīndra—the premonastic name of the Svāmī—was by nature indrawn, gentle and shy. The desire to pluck a nice flower in the Dakṣiṇeśvar garden brought him face to face with रामकृष्ण whom Yogin mistook for a gardener working there! He got the flower all right, but in the process, himself became a ‘flower plant’ to be tended by a great gardener of lives. Though married, the world could never drag his मिन्द् down to worldliness. Just as pure gold cannot be shaped into ornaments but has got to be alloyed with a small quantity of other metals, राम-कृष्ण had to ‘alloy’ him with a bit of harshness to counter his too gentle a personality that could not last in this mundane world. But the disciple was not a goody goody simpleton. He could exercise his highly critical discernment even against his own गुरु or leader (Svāmi Vivekānanda) when he thought it necessary. He was a good organizer. He had successfully attracted and inspired many a young man to the monastic life. He was extraordinarily devoted to the Holy मोथेर् whom he served till the last day of his life. His congenitally frail constitution could not stand the rigours he chose to impose upon himself resulting in a rather premature death on March 28, 1899.
16. Philosophy of Rāmakṛṣṇa
Introduction
Man is often described as a rational animal. Once the animal in him is reasonably satisfied by the provision of basic biological and some psychological needs, the rational part gets an opportunity to evolve to higher levels. Philosophy, including metaphysics, is one of the highest aspects of this evolution.
The Indian philosophical systems have developed not only as a result of intellectual speculations but also of mystical intuition. Hence the name ‘darśana’ (lit., ‘seeing’), usually applied to them. The topics most commonly discussed by these darśanas are generally four: the world and its च्रेअतिओन् or evolution; the existence, nature and attributes of the Absolute or God; the nature of man; and the goal of human life.
Different standpoints and differing views on these topics of discussion have naturally led to a variety of schools. These schools are broadly divided into two classes: the आस्तिक and the नास्तिक. The former accept the authority of the वेदस् whereas the latter do not. The वेदान्त दर्शन belongs to the former class and has gained a pre-eminent place in it due to its judicious combination of reasoning and acceptance of the authority of the वेदस् as also due to its long, unbroken tradition.
The word ‘Vedānta’ means the ‘end or essence of the वेदस्.’ The उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā (collectively known as the प्रस्थानत्रय), as also all other allied literature based on them, form the sources of Vedānta. Differing interpretations of the प्रस्थानत्रय, especially of the Brahma-sūtras, have given rise to different schools of Vedānta, of which Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत are well-known.
Advaita of Śaṅkara
Among these three schools, again it is the Advaita which has gained greater currency and is more widely known.
According to शङ्कर, the chief expounder of this school, the ultimate Truth is one and one only, and it is ब्रह्मन्. This ब्रह्मन् is Sat-Cit-आनन्द (‘Existence-Knowledge-Bliss-Absolute’) and is without form (nirākāra) and without attributes (nirguṇa). The world in which we live, move and have our being, is unreal since it is only an appearance in ब्रह्मन्, like that of a snake in a rope, due to इग्नोरन्चे or इल्लुसिओन्. However, as long as this इग्नोरन्चे or इल्लुसिओन् is not transcended and ब्रह्मन् is not realized as It is, this world of appearance, which is the ground of our experience, is given a tentative and empirical reality. When this empirical reality is admitted for the world, its च्रेअतिओन् or evolution, its sustenance, and its destruction or involution, have also to be admitted. Looked at from this angle and conceding ब्रह्मन् as the ground of evolution and involution of the world, It becomes ईश्वर or God, the supreme Ruler of च्रेअतिओन्. This ईश्वर creates, sustains and destroys the world out of his power of māyā.
As regard the individual souls, शङ्कर posits that they are really identical with ब्रह्मन्, their separate identity and bondage in the world being due to the इग्नोरन्चे (avidyā) of their real nature. This इग्नोरन्चे is beginningless (anādi) but can be ended through knowledge (jñāna) of their real nature as आत्मन् or Self identical with ब्रह्मन् or Absolute. Since it is इग्नोरन्चे (avidyā or अज्ञान) that has caused bondage for the individual सोउल्, शङ्कर maintains that knowledge (vidyā or ज्ञान) alone can give लिबेरतिओन्, though he admits that selfless action (niṣkāma कर्म) and devotion to God (bhakti) can be useful preliminary disciplines. In the state of लिबेरतिओन्, the individual Self merges in ब्रह्मन्, completely losing its identity.
Rāmakṛṣṇa’s Views
BRAHMAN
Now let us see how रामकृष्ण’s philosophy compares with that of शङ्कर. At the very outset, it has to be made clear that रामकृष्ण never propagated a system of philosophy of his own. He experienced the Truth directly and then spoke out of the fulness of that experience. Hence, we have to piece together his teachings on these aspects of philosophy given at random in his conversations.
Like शङ्कर, रामकृष्ण also accepts ब्रह्मन् as the highest and the only reality. He also accepts It as nirguṇa and nirākāra in Its aspect as the Absolute. But, unlike शङ्कर, he does not accept God (Īśvara), the aspect of ब्रह्मन् with form (sākāra) and with attributes (saguṇa), as either illusory or as a reality of a lower order. To him, God is both formless and possessed of form. Not only that, He is beyond both these too! Says he: ‘God is formless, and God is possessed of form too. And He is also that which transcends both form and formlessness. He alone knows what all He is.’ (Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna, 871).
He calls the Absolute as ब्रह्मन्, in Its eternal (nitya) aspect, i.e., when It is at rest and inactive. The same in Its sportive (līlā) aspect, when involved in the process of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction, he calls शक्ति or Kālī, the same as ईश्वर or God. So, according to him, ब्रह्मन् and शक्ति are one and inseparable. ‘The distinction between ब्रह्मन् and शक्ति is really a distinction without a difference. ब्रह्मन् and शक्ति are one (abhinna), just as fire and its burning power are one. ब्रह्मन् and शक्ति are one, just as milk and the whiteness of milk are one. ब्रह्मन् and शक्ति are one, just as a gem and its brightness are one. You cannot conceive of the one without the other, or make a difference between them.’ (ibid, 857.) ‘God the Absolute and God the Personal are one and the same. Belief in the one implies belief in the other. Fire cannot be thought of apart from its burning power, nor can its burning power be thought of apart from it. Again, the sun’s rays cannot be thought of apart from the sun, nor the sun, apart from its rays. You cannot think of the whiteness of milk apart from its milky whiteness. Thus the Absolute cannot be thought of apart from the idea of God with attributes, i.e., Personal God and vice versa.’ (ibid, 856.) ‘The Primordial Power and Supreme ब्रह्मन् are identical—it is like the snake and its wriggling motion.’ (The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, 1947 edn., p. 263)
MĀYĀ
Rāmakṛṣṇa accepts māyā as the veil that keeps God hidden from our sight. He compares it to a small patch of cloud that can hide the big sun from our view, or like the weeds that cover placid water. He also holds, like the Sāṅkhyas, that as soon as māyā is discovered, it disappears. But he is a little more considerate towards this māyā than the advaitins, because he accepts that it has two aspects, the विद्या-māyā and the अविद्या-māyā. The former helps a bound सोउल् to get लिबेरतिओन् by giving him discrimination and non-attachment. It is the latter, manifested as lust, lucre and egoism, that really binds him.
Again, this explanation which leads to the corollary that a spiritual aspirant should take recourse to विद्या-māyā to nullify the effects of अविद्या-māyā, even as one thorn (needle) is used to remove another thorn and then both are thrown away, adds a new dimension to the philosophy of spiritual practice (sādhanā). By ingeniously avoiding the need to propitiate a Personal God to remove this māyā, the purely Advaitic standpoint is maintained.
As regards the locus of māyā, there is no unanimity among the traditional advaitic schools. But रामकृष्ण solves the problem convincingly by saying that it is located in ब्रह्मन्, but acts on the individual souls (jīvas), like the poison of a snake which is contained in its mouth and yet does not affect it in any way, but acts on those bitten by it. He thus absolves ब्रह्मन् of any imperfection or limitation due to māyā.
CREATION
Coming to च्रेअतिओन्, रामकृष्ण gives it a much greater degree of reality than शङ्कर. He calls it the līlā aspect of ब्रह्मन् and hence real, though not eternal. It is like ice-crystals appearing on water and again dissolving back in water. The ice-crystals are as real as water, but do not endure permanently.
A person ascending the staircase to reach the roof of a building denies at first any ‘roofness’ to the stairs. But he discovers after reaching the roof that the stairs are also made of the same material as the roof. In the same way, though a man of wisdom (jñāni) may deny the world as not ब्रह्मन्, when he becomes a man of ‘supreme wisdom’ (vijñāni), through more complete realization, he accepts that the world is also ब्रह्मन्, since nothing exists apart from ब्रह्मन्. This theory gives us a greater insight with the help of which we can understand better, the activities of a jīvanmukta, one who is liberated even while living.
ĪŚVARA OR GOD
In शङ्कर’s Advaita, ब्रह्मन् the Absolute is not very responsive to human emotions or prayers. The ईश्वर we bank on is either unreal or has a precarious existence.
