But according to राम-कृष्ण, ईश्वर who is ब्रह्मन् in Its līlā-aspect, is real and responsive, and hence the entire gamut of devotional practices (bhakti-sādhanā) acquires validity and leads to fulfilment. Instead of being a secondary sādhanā, as in traditional advaita, भक्ति is a primary sādhanā placed on an equal footing with ज्ञान; and this is achieved within the broad framework of Advaita which both accept as the final truth.
Closely connected with this topic is the concept of the अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of God. शङ्कर, constrained by the extreme stance of advaita which he is obliged to adopt, is very apologetic about the whole doctrine (vide his commentary on the Bhagavadgītā 4.6-9). रामकृष्ण however has no such constraints since he accepts both the नित्य and the līlā aspects of ब्रह्मन् as equally real and valid. Once the līlā-aspect is accepted as real, there should be no difficulty at all in according reality to the अवतार of God also. God being omniscient and omnipotent, can do anything he likes. None can put any limitation on his power. If it is his will, he can be born as a human being and sport through it. In fact, he does sport through the human body to bring enlightenment to the bound souls, out of his infinite compassion for them. And again, since the इन्चर्नतिओन् is God Himself, seeing him is equivalent to seeing God. To touch the river गङ्गा, it is not necessary to touch the entire stretch of water from the Gomukh (the birth-place of the river) to the Gaṅgāsāgar (the place where the river joins the sea). It is enough if it is touched at Dakṣiṇeśvar!
IMMANENCE OF GOD
For शङ्कर the world is only an illusory appearance in ब्रह्मन्, like silver in nacre. ब्रह्मन् thus being the substratum of the world, appearance cannot be, strictly speaking, immanent in it. Immanence implies a much greater degree of reality for the substance in which immanence of the other is recognized. The उपनिषद्स् clearly speak of divine immanence in the world and the living beings (vide Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6; Aitareya Upaniṣad

). रामकृष्ण teaches not only of divine immanence in all beings and things but also of its manifestation in different degrees. Says he: ‘Every object is नारायण (i.e., God). Man is नारायण, the animal is नारायण, the sage is नारायण, the knave also is नारायण. All that exists is नारायण. The Deity (Nārāyaṇa) sports in various aspects. All things are his diverse forms and the manifestations of his glory.’ (Sayings, 890.) ‘God is in all men, but all men are not in God; that is why they suffer.’ (Sayings, 889.) ‘The manifestation of शक्ति (the Divine Power) varies in varying centres of activity; for variety is the law, not sameness. God is immanent in all creatures; he is even in the ant. The difference is in manifestation only.’ (Sayings, 892.)
JĪVA OR INDIVIDUAL SOUL
Coming to the nature of the जीव or man, रामकृष्ण admits that in his essential nature he is God Himself: ‘The सोउल् enchained is man, but when free from the chain (māyā), it is the Lord.’ (Sayings, 20) ‘What is the relation between the jīvātman and the परमात्मन्? As a current of water seems to be divided into two when a plank of wood is placed against it edgewise, so the Indivisible appears divided into two, the jīvātman and the परमात्मन्, due to the limitation of māyā.’ (Sayings, 21) ‘Water and a bubble on it are one and the same. The bubble has its birth in the water, floats on it, and is ultimately resolved into it. So also the jīvātman and the परमात्मन् are one and the same, the difference between them being only one of degree. For, one is finite and limited while the other is infinite; one is dependent while the other is independent.’ (Sayings, 22.)
CAUSE OF HIS BONDAGE
What then is it that causes his bondage? रामकृष्ण attributes it to egoism, brought about by the अविद्या-māyā. On a deeper analysis of this ‘I,’ it will be found to be non-existent even as nothing is leftover when we go on peeling an onion. And yet, it can create no end of troubles. Not only that, it is extremely difficult to get rid of! How then can we get rid of it? Classifying the ego into two groups, the ripe-ego and the unripe-ego, राम-कृष्ण advises us to cultivate the ripe-ego to counter the unripe one: ‘If you find that you cannot drive off this feeling of “I,” then let it remain as the “servant I.” There is not much to fear from the ego which is centred in the thought, “I am the servant of God, I am his devotee.” Sweets cause dyspepsia, but not sugar-candy which is an exception. The “servant I,” the “I” of a devotee, the “I” of a child—each of these is like a line drawn with a stick on the surface of water; this “I” does not last long.’ (ibid, 121.)
In this connection he gives the unique example as to how the liberated souls continue to live in this world and teach others even after their egoism has been wiped out: ‘As a piece of rope, when burnt, retains its form, but cannot serve to bind, so is the ego which is burnt by the fire of supreme knowledge.’ (ibid, 132.)
FOUR TYPES OF JĪVAS
Rāmakṛṣṇa, though conceding that all the jīvas, in the ultimate analysis, are equal, yet classifies them into four groups: the baddha (bound), the mumukṣu (struggling for लिबेरतिओन्), the mukta (emancipated) and the nityasiddha (ever-free).
Those of the last group are born to teach mankind. The first group is so deeply engrossed in the world of senses that it is least interested in the life of the spirit. The last two groups have already reached the goal of their lives. Hence it is the second group that needs special attention.
THE GOAL OF LIFE
Rāmakṛṣṇa says that the goal of life is God-realization. All our miseries will end, all our problems will be solved once for all, by realizing God. Following the ancient tradition, he advises the aspirants to seek a competent spiritual teacher (guru) first and then practise disciplines according to his directions. रामकृष्ण’s teachings contain a veritable mine of information and instructions on practical spiritual life. Unlike the traditional philo-sophies or religions, he is not at all dogmatic about the path leading to the goal. Just as the Kālighāṭ temple can be reached through several roads of Calcutta, God also can be realized through several spiritual paths and disciplines. In his philosophy of sādhanā, ज्ञान, भक्ति, योग and karma—all have a place. One can practise them either singly or in combination. What is needed is vyākulatā, great earnestness or intense longing. In fact, this approach of his can accommodate in its fold not only all the spiritual disciplines of हिन्दुइस्म्, but also those of other religions. He goes to the extent of according a place even to the abominable practices of some tāntrik schools, calling them as ‘backdoors,’ though he does not advocate or recommend them.
JÑĀNA OR भक्ति?
As regards the controversy among the various schools about ज्ञान or भक्ति being the direct path to लिबेरतिओन्, राम-कृष्ण advocates devotion tempered by knowledge (jñāna-miśrita-भक्ति) as most suitable for this age. This standpoint avoids the extremes and prevents the aspirant from becoming dry or sentimental, the dangers to which he is generally exposed if he follows only one of them to the exclusion of the other.
What happens to a person when he realizes God? Here, रामकृष्ण follows the traditional description given in the scriptures. The man of realization experiences unalloyed bliss within and sees the Divine everywhere. Outwardly he may not exhibit any signs of his inner joy and may even behave like an abnormal person. But one thing is certain: He remains unaffected by the vicissitudes of life which affect others intensely. He lives in God and works for the good of others, seeing God in them.
CONTINUANCE OF BODY AFTER REALIZATION
Rāmakṛṣṇa says that normally a person who goes into nirvikalpa समाधि (the highest state of superconsciousness) remains in that state for twenty-one days and then passes away. However, a few who are destined to teach mankind, return to the ordinary plane of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् by keeping a trace of egoism without which corporeal existence is impossible.
About prārabdha-कर्म (the result of past deeds, that have borne fruit in this life) रामकृष्ण accepts it as inevitable but assures us that a greater part of its effects can be offset by the power of God’s name (vide Teachings of Sri Ramakrishna, 913).
PROBLEM OF GOOD AND EVIL
Concerning the problem of good and evil which has been debated much in philosophy, रामकृष्ण says that the very act of च्रेअतिओन् presupposes imperfection. Just as pure gold cannot be made into ornaments unless it is mixed with traces of baser metals, the world cannot come into existence without māyā. The simultaneous existence of good and evil is to be counteracted through good as far as possible. But the ultimate solution is to transcend both good and evil by rising to supreme spiritual heights where everything is levelled in God. Then neither good nor evil is recognized, just as it is impossible to notice the difference in the heights of tall trees or clusters of grass when one is flying high in the sky.
CAUSE OF DISAGREEMENT
Finally, a word about why there is so much disagreement and difference among the various philosophical systems and religions. रामकृष्ण tackles this question from two standpoints: the subjective and the objective. Through the well-known story of the blind men and the elephant, he tells us that when people get an incomplete or imperfect view of God and preach it as the whole truth, conflicts are bound to appear. This is from the subjective standpoint. From the objective standpoint, he says that God is so great that none can comprehend him fully. He alone knows what all he is. ब्रह्मन् or God is the one thing that has not become ‘ucchiṣṭa’ (food tasted and leftover) since none has till now fully described him. Any attempt to size him up with our limited intellect and describe him through our limited speech will be as futile as the efforts of the salt-doll that wanted to gauge the depths of the sea! Hence, even when people who have had genuine and complete spiritual experience try to describe him (who is really indescribable), their descriptions are bound to fall far short of the ideal and are also apt to be different from one another.
Conclusion
In conclusion we can safely assert that रामकृष्ण’s experiences and utterances, though similar in many respects to the traditional Vedānta, have much more in them that can form the subject matter for a fascinating study, unravelling new vistas of Vedānta. After all, this is how Sanātana धर्म has grown over the millennia!

Rāma-pūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् assigned to the Atharvaṇaveda and devoted to the cult of राम. There are 94 verses in the anuṣṭubh metre spread over five chapters, each being known as ‘Upaniṣad.’
The first chapter with 13 verses gives several interesting definitions of the word ‘Rāma.’ Two of them are:
One by whom the राक्षसस् (rā) are killed (māraṇa; ma).
One in whom the yogins find pleasure (ramante).
The second chapter with only three verses describes how the whole universe has come out of the seed ‘Rāma,’ even as the banyan tree comes out of its tiny seed.
The third chapter describes the whole universe as a यन्त्र (geometrical representation) of राम and his spouse सीता. Obeisance to them with the word namaḥ is itself the मन्त्र (esoteric formula).
The fourth chapter with 67 verses is the longest. The subjects dealt with in this are:
The six-syllabled मन्त्र of राम (as indicated in the Rāmarahasyopaniṣad 2.16-24); a prayer to राम by gods for the destruction of their enemies; prayer by the ṛṣis or sages which gives the story of Rāmā in brief; a beautiful description of राम, after being crowned as the king; details of inscribing the Rāmayantra (mystical diagram infused with the spirit of राम); mālāmantra consisting of 48 letters, beginning with Om namo bhagavate raghunandanāya and ending with viṣṇave namaḥ; and, the eulogy of the यन्त्र.
The last section with ten verses deals with some ritualistic aspects connected with भूतशुद्धि (purification of elements), worship of the पीठ or the base, meditation on the Lord or God and attainment of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् by his grace.

Rāmaliṅga
(‘the शिवलिङ्ग [established by] राम’)
------------------------------------------
The लिङ्ग in the main temple of शिव at one of the most sacred places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, Rāmeśvara, is called ‘Rāmaliṅga’.
There are two versions in the पुराणस् regarding the establishment of this लिङ्ग.
When राम was building the bridge on the sea, रावण used to come every night and demolish it. To prevent this, राम built a शिव temple and established the शिवलिङ्ग, at the entrance to the bridge. Since रावण was a staunch devotee of शिव, he could no longer destroy the bridge!
According to a second story, राम decided to build a temple for शिव to atone for the killing of रावण (who was a ब्राह्मण). When he was returning from लङ्का in the Puṣpakavimāna (the divine aeroplane), he alighted at the place (now known as Rāmeśvara) and expressed this desire to his divine spouse सीता. She then prepared a लिङ्ग out of sea-sand which was duly consecrated by राम.
As per another version, हनुमान् had been sent to वाराणसी (Kāśī) to bring a लिङ्ग. Since he was late in returning and since the auspicious moment was coming to an end, सीता prepared the लिङ्ग and राम consecrated it. The लिङ्ग brought later by हनुमान् was also established in another place nearby (now known as Viśvaliṅga). To pacify him राम made it a rule that pilgrims should worship that लिङ्ग first and then only visit the main shrine.
See also RĀMEŚVARA.

India seems to have a special knack of producing great saints almost on a ‘made to order’ basis, as per the needs of the times.
When शङ्कर’s (A.

-820) Advaita Vedānta was being misinterpretated and misused, there was a great need to restore the balance between true ज्ञान (spiritual wisdom) and genuine भक्ति (devotion to God sans sentimentalism). It was during this critical period that Rāmānuja’s advent took place.
RāmānujācāryaRāmānuja (considered by his followers as a reincarnation of लक्ष्मण, the younger brother of राम) was born as the son of Āsūri Keśava Dīkṣita and Kānti-matī at Śrīperumbudūr, 48 kms. (30 miles) to the south-west of Madras or Chennai, the present capital of Tamil Nadu.
Endowed with a sharp intellect and a prodigious memory, he was well-educated even at a young age.
Keśava Dīkṣita got him married at the age of sixteen, as was the custom during those days. Soon after this, Keśava Dīkṣita passed away, plunging the whole family in grief.
Partly to forget the grief of bereavement, but mainly for the higher एदुचतिओन् of Rāmānuja, the family now shifted to the well-known town of काञ्चीपुरम्. Rāmānuja now started his higher studies under यादवप्रकाश, a Vedāntic scholar of repute during those days.
Yādavaprakāśa’s leanings towards dry monism, bereft of devotion to a Personal God, soon brought him into intellectual conflicts with Rāmānuja whose genius and deeply devotional temperament could not be countered by him. After a few unfortunate incidents and encounters, Rāmānuja had to leave him for good.
Meanwhile Rāmānuja’s name had become so well-known that यामुनाचार्य, the chief pontiff of the श्रीवैष्णव (a sect of Vaiṣṇavas or worshippers of विष्णु) monastery at श्रीरङ्गम् (a famous temple-town on the bank of the river कावेरी in Tamil Nadu) had decided to take him as his successor. However, he died before he could carry out his wish. It so happened that Rāmānuja reached the बुरिअल् ground before the body was consigned to the earth, but found three fingers of his right hand clenched. Learning of the dead-saint’s last desires—three in number and unfulfilled during his lifetime—he openly promised before the gathering of mourners to fulfil all of them. And lo! the three fingers opened out!
The following were those promises:
Remaining in the Vaiṣṇava fold, I shall arrange for a commentary to be written on the Tiruvāymoḷi of नम्माऌवार्.
I shall write a commentary on the Brahmasūtras of बादरायण.
In honour of the great sage पराशर, who wrote the Viṣṇupurāṇa, I shall leave behind a great Vaiṣṇava by that name.
Rāmānuja had been in close touch with Kāñcīpūrṇa, a great devotee of God, whose company he often sought and felt inspired. However, since he belonged to the śūdra caste, Rāmānuja’s wife Rakṣāmbāḷ treated him with disdain. This, as also other incidents that revealed his wife’s innate incapacity to rise to the higher levels of his own psychological make-up, made Rāmānuja renounce the world and take सṁन्यास (monastic orders) at काञ्चीपुरम् in front of the temple of वरदराज (Viṣṇu), assuming the new name ‘Yatirāja’.
He then retired to श्रीरङ्गम्, settled down there and studied many Vaiṣṇava texts under the guidance of an outstanding scholar of those times, Mahāpūrṇa. He also received the sacred aṣṭākṣarīmantra (eight-syllabled मन्त्र of नारायण) from the great saint गोष्ठीपूर्ण who also forbade him from revealing it to anyone else. Strangely enough, the very first act of Rāmānuja was to announce it loudly to one and all from the tower of a way-side temple, much to the chagrin of his गुरु गोष्ठीपूर्ण. When Rāmānuja confessed his ‘guilt’ but explained that he was prepared to go to हेल्ल् because of this sacrilegious act, if the listeners of the मन्त्र would instantly be liberated, the गुरु was dumb-founded and fell at his feet!
At the command of God (Raṅganātha) Rāmānuja took over the management of the temple of श्रीरङ्गम् and reorganised it very efficiently. This raised the animo-sity of some priests who had their own axes to grind. However, all their machinations to harm him were set at naught by divine grace.
During his long stay at श्रीरङ्गम्, Rāmānuja was able to win many disciples, quite a few of whom were weaned away from other schools and sects to वैष्णविस्म्.
He also trained in his मठ (mona-stery), seventy-four pious householders to become family gurus to the general run of devotees and followers.
As promised before the dead-body of यामुनाचार्य, Rāmānuja wrote the Śrībhāṣya, a detailed commentary on the Brahmasūtras (or Vedāntasūtras) of बादरायण (Vyāsa) according to theistic (Vaiṣṇavite) philosophy, now well-known as Viśiṣṭādvaita. For this he had to travel all the way to Kāśmīra where the only manuscript of a famous ancient commentary by the sage बोधायन was available and which formed the basis for his work. He was lucky to get its help.
He thus fulfilled the most important of the three promises he had given to the सोउल् of यामुनाचार्य.
He had already fulfilled the first promise by his discourses on the Tiruvāy-moḷi of नम्माऌवार् and by giving the Divyaprabandhams (See प्रबन्धम्">DIVYAPRABAN-DHAM for details.) a status equal to that of the Sanskrit scriptures.
As regards the third, it was fulfilled by giving the name पराशरभट्ट, to the son of his prominent disciple कूरेश and urging him to write a bhāṣya or commentary on the well-known hymn of विष्णु, the Viṣṇusahasranāma, thereby perpetuating the memory of the great sage पराशर (father of वेदव्यास and composer of the Viṣṇupurāṇa).
During his stay at श्रीरङ्गम् in Tamil Nadu, Rāmānuja had to face the wrath of the fanatical Śaiva king Kulottuṅga. To escape from him, Rāmānuja migrated to मेल्कोटे near the city of Mysore where he, later on, built a nice temple of विष्णु (known as Celuva-नारायण or Śelvapiḷḷai). Since the people of the depressed castes had helped him to recover the original (ancient) image buried under a mound, which he later established in the temple, he gave them the privilege of entering the temple for a vision of the Lord, for three days every year. This was a revolutionary step for those days of rabid casteism.
Before he returned to श्रीरङ्गम् after the demise of Kulottuṅga, an image of his was installed in the मेल्कोटे temple premises, with his consent. A similar image was also installed at Śrīperumbu-dūr, his birthplace.
He spent his last days at श्रीरङ्गम् itself and passed away peacefully during the month of Māgha (January-February) in A.

.
The greatest contribution of Rāmānuja was to preach and establish a religio-philosophical system that gave equal importance to ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion).
Rāmānuja wrote (in Sanskrit) eight works in all, of which the Śrībhāṣya was the magnum opus.
The other seven are: Vedārtha Saṅgraha (a compendium of important statements from the major उपनिषद्स् with his own interpretation, according to the Viśiṣṭādvaita school); Vedāntadīpa and Vedāntasāra (abridged commentaries on the Vedāntasūtras or the Brahmasūtras); Gītābhāṣya; Nityagrantha dealing with the daily rituals and devotional practices for his followers; the three hymnal works in prose, known as the Gadyatraya.
The three components of the Gadyatraya are: Śaraṇāgatigadya (dealing with the greatness of self-surrender); Śrīraṅgagadya (prayer to God to accept him as his eternal servant); Vaikuṇṭhagadya (a description of वैकुण्ठ, the world of विष्णु).
Rāmānuja’s great contribution lies in his bringing together the Vedic ideology and methodology rooted in the Sanskrit scriptural texts and the purely devotional heritage of the आऌवार्स् (See ĀḶVĀRS.), thus creating what is now called the ‘Ubhaya-Vedānta,’ ‘Vedānta based on two traditions’.
The Vedānta system of Rāmānuja is known as the Viśiṣṭādvaita दर्शन. It is advaita or monism but viśiṣṭa or qualified. According to him ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute) is the highest and independent reality. अचित् (insentient nature, also known as प्रकृति) and cit (the conscious beings, the jīvas or individual souls) are also eternal realities but dependent on ब्रह्मन् who includes them and also transcends them.
Brahman is the Supreme Person (Sarveśvara) endowed with infinite auspicious qualities. He is responsible for सृष्टि (creation), sthiti (maintenance) and प्रलय (dissolution) of this world.
The jīvas are atomic in size and infinite in number. They are different from the body and possess चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् as an attribute.
The aspirants desirous of attaining मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् must start with the performance of prescribed karmas or duties. This leads to the purification of their minds making them fit to tread the spiritual path of ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion), including प्रपत्ति (self-surrender).
Acit is the insentient matter, the matrix of the world, out of which the physical universe is created.
The liberated jīvas live in Paramapada or वैकुण्ठ, the special abode of the Lord नारायण, with divine bodies, eternally enjoying his company. They will never again return to this mundane existence.

-1581)
------------------------------------------
Guru Rāmdās was the fourth of the ten Gurus of सिखिस्म्.
He was the son of Haridās, a shopkeeper, and Anūp देवी who was also known as दया Kaur. They belonged to the Khatrī caste.
He was born in Chuna Mandi in Lahore district (now in Pakistan). He was given the name Jeṭhā.
He lost both the parents when he was just seven years and was brought up by his grandmother in her village Basarke.
He lived by selling cooked beans in the market place.
At the age of twelve, he shifted to Goindvāl, a new habitation founded by गुरु Amardās (A.

-1574). Very soon he attracted the attention of the गुरु whom he joined and started serving him with great sincerity and devotion. The गुरु, being pleased by it, gave him his daughter Bībī Bhānī in मर्रिअगे. The couple stayed at Goindvāl itself so that they could serve the गुरु.
Gradually Jeṭhā came to be known as Rāmdās.
The couple had three sons: Prīticand, Mahādev and Arjandev.
Once, गुरु Amardās sent him to Lahore to meet the Mughal Emperor Akbar (A.

-1605) who was camping there, to clear some wrong notions about the teachings of the गुरु. He fulfilled this assignment admirably.
Before passing away गुरु Amardās had chosen Rāmdās as his successor and had instructed him to construct a pool in the land specially acquired for that purpose. It was 40 kms. (25 miles) to the northwest of Goindvāl. Gradually a town also came up around the pool. This is the now famous city of Amritsar with its pool round the गोल्देन् तेम्प्ले.
Guru Rāmdās had to take a lot of trouble to complete the work due to lack of funds. However he finally succeeded in the same.
Another contribution of the गुरु was the establishment of ‘Mañjīs’ or preaching centres. The Sikh brotherhood was divided into 22 mañjīs. They had special couches on which pious Sikh teachers would sit and preach the tenets of सिखिस्म्.
Guru Rāmdās was a great poet. The Guru Grantha Sāhib contains 638 hymns of his in 30 rāgas (musical tunes). They are full of the praise of God and his name as also a sādhaka’s yearning for God.
He passed away in 1581 after anointing his last son Arjandev, since he was the most devoted and faithful disciple.

Rāma
(‘one who gives delight [to the yogis]’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu epics and the पुराणस्, three Rāmas are dealt with: राम the son of दशरथ (also known as श्रीराम), राम of the battle-axe (called परशु-राम) and राम, the strong (or बलराम).
See BALARĀMA, PARAŚURĀMA and RĀMĀYAṆA for details.

Rāmottaratāpanīya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This Upaniṣad is a continuation of the Pūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad. Here, राम is described as निर्विशेष ब्रह्मन् (Brahman without attributes), whereas in the former he is described as saviśeṣa (with attributes) to facilitate meditation by devotees.
The whole text which is in the form of a dialogue between the sage Yājña-valkya and some sages like बृहस्पति, भरद्वाज and अत्रि, contains 121 verses, including passages in prose, spread over five khaṇḍas or chapters.
The first khaṇḍa with three passages, describes the importance of कुरुक्षेत्र and Avimukta (same as काशी or वाराणसी), their sacredness and their identity with the space in between the eyebrows inside us.
The belief that शिव utters the tāraka-मन्त्र (“Rāma”) into the ears of the dying persons is alluded to.
The second khaṇḍa with 19 verses and prose sections, deals with the power of the राम-ṣaḍakṣara-मन्त्र (= rāṁ rāmāya namaḥ) as tāraka or endowed with liberatingpower and is compared with ओङ्कार or प्रणव. That a sādhaka who repeats it daily is freed from all sins, is also stated.
There is also an interesting description of the प्रणव as representing राम, लक्ष्मण, भरत, शत्रुघ्न as also सीता.
Seven mantras (1 to 7) of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad find a place in this section.
The third khaṇḍa (16 passages) starts by stating that the आत्मन् who is infinite bliss is realised by meditating on it in the space between the eyebrows, above the nose.
It then describes how शिव performed austerities like जप (repetition of राम’s name), arcana (worship) and होम (oblations into a duly consecrated fire) to please राम and how राम appeared before him and granted him his desire that all those who die (including animals or even worms) on the Maṇikarṇikā-ghāṭ on the bank of the river गङ्गा in काशी should get लिबेरतिओन्. For this, शिव had only to utter Rāmamantra in the ear of the dead being.
The fourth khaṇḍa with 49 paras and verses, deals with a number of mantras (each with 40 letters), partly resembling the Gāyatrīmantra.
The fifth or the last khaṇḍa with 34 verses and paras, describes the greatness of the Rāmaṣaḍakṣara-मन्त्र, eulogising it in 24 verses as far superior to other mantras, of deities like गणपति, शिव, देवी and even विष्णु!

------------------------------------------
One of the well-known Hindu religious leaders of recent times, Svāmi रामतीर्थ was born in a small village Miraliwala of Punjab (now in Pakistan) as the second son of Gosvāmi Hīrānanda, who was a poor ब्राह्मण priest. His original name was Gosvāmi Tīrtharāṁ. He lost his मोथेर् at an early age and was brought up by his elder brother and sister-in-law.
Thanks to his sharp intellect, he got a good एदुचतिओन् not only in Sanskrit, Urdu and Persian, but also in Vedānta, under competent teachers like Dharmārām and Bābā Nagīnsiṁha Vedī in Gujaranwala.
In his twentythird year, he became a professor of mathematics in the Foreman Christian College of Lahore (now in Pakistan).
Religious by nature and given to contemplation on God, he was deeply influenced by Svāmi Vivekānanda (A.

-1902) when the latter visited Lahore.
Though married at a young age, he left the family in A.

, and took सṁन्यास (monastic life) assuming the new name Svāmi रामतीर्थ. After performing severe austerities in the हिमालयस् he returned to his native place and then travelled to Japan and the U.S.A. where he lectured on the Vedānta. His pure life, attractive personality and oratory made him quite popular.
He wrote a number of articles on the need to attain political freedom.
He always stressed two things: not accepting anything without proper reasoning; and, working for the good of others, especially our motherland.
Himself possessing a strong physique he also advocated exercising the body as equally import for spiritual life and service to mankind.
He died by drowning in the river गङ्गा, probably of his own accord, in A.

Ramakrishna Order, The
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Right from the age of the उपनिषद्स्, the Hindu society had sheltered and protected the saṁnyāsins from the problems and worries of the world, and had taken care of them so well that they could pursue their chosen path towards perfection unhindered.
However, the barbaric invasions from outside by the Mohammedans (A.
) and the wily manoeuvres as also the stick and carrot policy of the English (since A.

) gradually undermined the Hindu society to such an extent that it badly needed resuscitation at the hands of people totally dedicated to the Hindu cause. Though the various reform-movements like the Brahma Samāj and the Ārya Samāj contributed their bit to the revival and strengthening of the Hindu society, their approach fell short of the requirements, since they had ignored the all-comprehensive evolution of हिन्दुइस्म् over the past millenniums and were in too great a hurry to reform according to their own favourite theories.
Belur Math Temple ViewHence there had arisen a great need to dehypnotise the society from adopting partial or alien means, and to resurrect it by utilising the age-old, time-tested, methods of ज्ञान (spiritual wisdom) and तपस् (austerity).
Rāmakṛṣṇa, the Architect
This is exactly what रामकृष्ण (A.

-1886)—more well-known as Śrī रामकृष्ण परमहṁस and worshipped by millions of his devotees as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of God—did during his rather short life of fifty years. He first practised vigorously all the spiritual disciplines of the various facets of हिन्दुइस्म् and came to the conclusion that they led to the same mystical experience of ब्रह्मन्/Ātman as described in the उपनिषद्स् and allied scriptures. An extension of his efforts towards some alien religions also corroborated the same experience.
It is this universal experience that made him declare, ‘As many faiths, so many paths!’
Though equipped with this magni-ficent weapon of ज्ञान (highest spiritual wisdom) gained through तपस् (single minded austerities), रामकृष्ण knew very well that the task of regeneration of the सनातनधर्म (the Eternal Religion or हिन्दुइस्म्) and uplifting this country—the भारतवर्ष or Bhārata, the homeland of spiritual wisdom for aeons—was a task that would extend beyond the normal span of human life and would need the wholehearted cooperation of a well-knit band of dedicated disciples.
Birth of the Order
This is precisely what he did when he gathered and trained his young disciples with Narendranāth (future Vivekā-नन्द) as their anointed leader. It is these disciples—who were also blessed with monastic robes by रामकृष्ण himself—that formed the core of a new monastic order that bears his name now.
They were sixteen in number and were the founders of this order. After taking formal monastic vows through appropriate rituals they, under the guidance of Narendranāth or Vivekānanda (A.

-1902), assumed new names as follows:
Bāburām Svāmi Premānanda (A.

-1899)

The Motto and the Emblem
Any organisation, especially the one that bears the name of an epoch-making person, needs a motto to guide it and an emblem that constantly reminds and inspires. Realising this, Vivekānanda placed before it the motto: ātmano mokṣārthaṁ jagaddhitāya ca (‘For the लिबेरतिओन् of the Self and service to the society’). He also designed a charming but distinctive emblem that effectively reflected this motto. It consists of an elegant swan against the backdrop of the rising sun, surrounded by wavy waters from which has arisen a beautiful lotus flower along with a couple of leaves. This whole picture is encircled by a hooded serpent.
Whereas the motto adds a social dimension to the hitherto, purely personal, aspect of a self-centred sādhana, the emblem—which graphically describes a balanced combination or harmony of all the four yogas—enriches that sādhanā by making it more comprehensive.
The Bifurcation
The basic philosophy of life put before the Ramakrishna Order by Vivekānanda automatically led to a bifurcation of its activities into two important, but parallel, areas. The ātmamokṣa aspect resulted in the establishment of the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ्, an organisation catering predominantly to the spiritual needs of the मोन्क्स् of the order as also its votaries. The jagaddhita aspect on the other hand, gave rise to another, a sister organisation, concentrating solely on public service activities.
Legal Formalities
Though the Ramakrishna Order of मोन्क्स् was started in A.
itself with its first monastery at Baranagore in Calcutta (now Kolkata), in a dilapidated होउसे, it was shifted to its own campus in Belur, only in A.
, primarily due to the untiring efforts of Vivekānanda. For some time (A.

-1899) it had been housed in the Alambazaar area of Calcutta also.
The रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् was legally registered as a trust in A.
and the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् in A.

.
The रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् Association which Vivekānanda himself had formally established on the 1st of May 1897, later on went out of existence, once the other two institutions were given a legal shape.
Some of the aims and objects contemplated in the original Association were as follows:
Preaching the truths taught by राम-कृष्ण, based on his life and experiences; to bring about fellowship among the followers of different religious; to train men to become competent to teach spiritual knowledge as well as secular sciences for the welfare of the masses; to encourage arts and industries; to establish maṭhas and āśramas (monasteries) in different parts of India for training saṁnyāsins; to send trained saṁnyāsins to foreign countries to bring about a better understanding between them and India; to totally eschew politics; any other spiritual and humanitarian activities in consonance with these ideals.
The fairly fast evolution of the order into two distinct fields of work—spiritual ministry and social service—made its two wings grow into two parallel organisations. Hence it is necessary to consider them here in greater detail.
The Ramakrishna Math
The रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् is a purely monastic organisation, totally dedicated to the twin ideals of त्याग (renouncing everything for the sake of spiritual enlightenment) and sevā (service to living beings as worship of God Himself).
Young men eligible for joining the monastic order as per the prescribed rules of admission (which can be obtained from any centre of the Ramakrishna Order) are vigorously trained by competent senior मोन्क्स् over a period of nearly ten years after which they are initiated into सṁन्यास (monastic life) if found fit.
Insistence on meditation, study of scriptures and austerities in personal life, and, on service activities as worship of God through human beings in social life, will help these novices to be shaped into ideal मोन्क्स् in course of time.
Unlike the old monastic orders, the Ramakrishna Monastic Movement has certain unique features. They may be listed as follows:
A. Non-sectarian
Though rooted firmly in the ancient Hindu monastic ideals of chastity and absence of possessions, it has avoided identification with any particular sect or group or even tradition. It embraces the whole gamut of religio-spiritual development of the entire Hindu race over the last five millennia or more. Not only that, it has provided a place in itself for the people of alien religions and cultures too, provided they are prepared to follow the basic monastic disciplines as exemplified in the lives of Ramakrishna-Vivekananda. In fact, the word ‘alien’ is itself alien to the Ramakrishna-Vivekananda culture!
B. Austerity, Learning and Missionary Zeal
Śaṅkara, the earliest pioneer of orga-nized Hindu मोनस्तिचिस्म्, insisted that his disciples, who were abbots of his monasteries, keep alive the spirit of तपस् (austerity) and ज्ञान (learning) in their personal lives and undertake pravāsa (tours) for the sake of pracāra (dissemination of धर्म or righteousness) for public good. Vivekānanda who realized the wisdom of this healthy convention set up by शङ्कर, has ordained that it be followed in his monastic order too. The Ramakrishna Order is sincerely trying to keep up this glorious tradition.
C. Group Life and Work Ethic
But, unlike the old Hindu मोनस्तिचिस्म् which insisted upon a lonely life, the new monastic movement advocates living in a group, thus forging a Saṅgha (organisation). This itself has several advantages, the greatest being the strengthening of one another’s spiritual vibrations, and the rounding off of one’s angularities. Is not community life itself a great discipline?
Its philosophy of service, of serving the जीव (the individual सोउल्) as शिव (God), has elevated the act of service—which would have stagnated, at best, at the level of social service—to the sublime levels of spiritual practice. This automatically helps the members of the Saṅgha in their personal spiritual evolution too.
Its insistence on work ethic, especially on high quality work, of which punctuality and punctiliousness are hallmarks, has set a model to the people of our country. If followed properly, it can bring the Kingdom of हेअवेन् to this earth.
Its active canvassing for the total development of the human society in particular, by adopting all healthy means at our disposal, including science and technology as also sound and time-tested economic principles, is another unique feature that distinguishes it from the old monastic systems which kept aloof from the social life in all its aspects, though deriving all benefits from the society!
D. Attitude towards Social Reform
It is true that this monastic movement does not directly involve itself in social reform activities. But, by quietly working for man-making and character-building, by inculcating the right values and attitudes in the minds of men, it is actually helping the society to carry out ‘root and branch reform’ as Vivekānanda put it.
E. Attitude towards Politics
However, Vivekānanda the prophet of modern India, with an uncanny vision of the future, forbade his organization strictly from taking part in any political movement or activity. Why? Because the monk is a world-citizen, nay, a man of God! (And, world-citizens do not dabble in politics, whereas Godmen have no politics at all.) Even though this decision of his was not relished by some of the participants of the early years of freedom movement, later history has proved that he was absolutely right. Not only that, almost all the great national leaders were inspired by his speeches and writings.
Some facts may now be adduced here to give an idea of the work that is being done by the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् institutions:
NATURE OF WORK : ritualistic worship of रामकृष्ण, the presiding deity; personal interviews to aspirants giving the necessary spiritual guidance; celebration of all important Hindu festivals as also the birthdays of the great religious leaders of हिन्दुइस्म्; publication of Hindu religious works and journals; preaching of religio-spiritual subjects often related to or based on the life and teachings of रामकृष्ण as also his monastic disciples; running of libraries of religio-philosophical literature; special programmes for the youth to supplement their एदुचतिओन् with moral and spiritual values and so on.
CENTRES : There were 53 centres of the Math including 18 in foreign countries in April 2003.
The Ramakrishna Mission
Unlike the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ्, the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् is a public institution admitting lay members too, who subscribe to its philosophy and policies. The individual centres, though run by the monastic members, generally have a Managing Committee with non-monastic lay devotees also. The work of these centres is spread over the following fields:
Running of schools, colleges and hostels for students; starting and managing medical institutions like dispensaries, hospitals and medical camps; rural welfare activities including integrated rural development schemes; relief and rehabilitation measures during periods of natural or manmade calamities like famines, floods, earthquakes, riots, fire-disasters, cyclones and so on.
CENTRES : There were in all in April 2003, 59 centres of the Mission including 8 in foreign lands.
In addition to these, there were 25 combined Math and Mission centres, of which 6 were outside India.
The foreign countries where these centres are located are: Argentina, Australia, Bangladesh, Canada, Fiji, France, Japan, Malaysia, Mauritius, Netherlands, Russia, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Switzerland, United Kingdom and United States of America.
Administration
The Math is managed by the Trustees who are all senior मोन्क्स् of the Order and the Mission by a Governing Body whose members are the same as the Trustees, the distinction made being purely for legal purposes.
After ascertaining the opinions of the senior मोन्क्स् of the Order, the Trustees elect from among themselves a President, one to three Vice-presidents, a General Secretary and four Assistant Secretaries.
The President—also called the ‘Saṅghaguru’—is the supreme Head of the whole organisation and the sole authority for giving सṁन्यास or administering the vows of monastic life.
He and the Vice-presidents are also empowered to grant mantradīkṣā (initiation into spiritual life) to devotees aspiring for it.
The General Secretary is the administrative head of the organisation. However, his power is limited to implementing the decisions taken by the Trustees/Members of the Governing Body, though he has the freedom to act in matters of day-to-day administration. The assistant secretaries work under his guidance.
The individual centres of the Math are managed by the presidents and of the Mission, by the secretaries, duly appointed by the Trustees/Members of the Governing Body. These again, are expected to carry on their work with the assistance of the monastic members allotted to their centres as also volunteers and paid-workers.
The funds needed for running the various institutions are raised by public donations and government grants wherever possible. Fees and charges may also be collected from well-to-do persons, for the services rendered, especially in educational and medical centres. Sale of religious books and allied literature as also various agricultural and rural products may also be another source of income.
Spreading the Message
The main purpose of the Rama-krishna-Vivekananda Movement—as it is designated today—is to spread the central message of रामकृष्ण-Vivekānanda, as expressed through the motto of the Rama-krishna Order.
Apart from its various centres which are relentlessly working towards this goal, a large number of institutions have been started by the devotees, friends and admirers of the Order on their own. These institutions which are generally called ‘Private Centres’, and are not legally affiliated to the Headquarters of the order, are being run under the guidance of the मोन्क्स् of the order, following the same pattern of activities.
The process of legally bringing such centres under the general umbrella of protection and policy of the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् started in A.

and is slowly but satisfactorily progressing. This umbrella organisation has been named ‘Ramakrishna-Vivekananda-Bhavaprachara Parishat’ and is being formed in each of the States of India. This has brought in greater cohesiveness in the working of such private centres and also generated deeper faith in the minds of the public who are assisting in their working.
Each of these centres, as a policy, is organising an annual conference of all the devotees of that State. This is naturally bringing them together and making them feel that they belong to one spiritual family.
Centres in Foreign Countries
The centres of the Ramakrishna Order in foreign lands fall into two broad categories. Those countries where the social situation is similar to that of India like Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Fiji or Mauritius, the nature of service activities is also similar. In other countries, especi-ally America, Canada and of Europe, the work is confined mostly to the preaching of Vedānta, publication of books and journals and personal guidance in spiritual matters.
It is gratifying to note that persons of these western countries also are showing a lot of interest in रामकृष्ण-Vivekā-नन्द Literature and are even opting for monastic life in the Order.
Epilogue
Within a short span of 117 years (A.

-2003), the Ramakrishna Movement has grown into a formidable force influencing the lives of millions of persons interested in personal peace of मिन्द् and social harmony.
Absence of narrow, sectarian or fana-tical approach to religion, an all-comprehensive view of life stressing spiritual evolution of man rather than the dogmatic side of religious observances, and a genuine attitude of service to man as service to God have endeared this Movement to one and all.
If the decent and dignified behaviour of the well-educated and cultured monastics of the Order has given the organisation its good image, no less is the contribution of the volunteers, the devotees and the well-wishers to its phenomenal growth.
No wonder then, that it has been widely recognised as having added a new dimension to Hindu मोनस्तिचिस्म् and played a significant role in the renaissance of हिन्दुइस्म्.

Rāmāyaṇa ------------------------------------------ 1. Introduction If there is one holy book that has profoundly influenced the life, the thought and the culture of millions of Hindus over the millennia, it is, undoubtedly, the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि. No aspect of Hindu religion and culture, whether it is literature, drama, मुसिच्, art or sculpture, has remained unaffected by it. There also seems to be, apparently, no place in the Indian sub-continent that has not had the privilege of being visited by राम and सीता or लक्ष्मण and हनुमान्! This rock contains the footprint of राम; that mountain split into two, unable to bear the weight of हनुमान्; the water of this rivulet is coloured since सीता had washed her clothes—this is how, even now, the simple folk of rural India weave an affectionate bond between themselves and the immaculate heroes of the Rāmāyaṇa. Hence, a reverent study of this wonderful work can certainly contribute to the levelling up of our culture in the social field and add an inch or two to our inner evolution and elevation. 2. Historicity of the राम Story There is a fundamental difference between the Occidental and the Hindu concepts of history. For the former, an incident that had really occurred, its date or time or period as also the location, is all-important. An implement of stone, a piece of pottery or an ancient coin discovered during archaeological excavations are more valuable as ‘evidence’ for the existence or the occurrence of that incident than whether it has left its imprint on the future generations or not. On the other hand, the existence of persons or the occurrence of incidents in the past are completely ignored by the Hindu psyche if they have not had any impact—good or bad—on the life and manners or the culture of the future generations. Another basic difference should also be noted. If the West looks at time as a linear thing with a beginning and an end, the Hindu मिन्द् views it as cyclic and hence without beginning or end. The division of time into युगस् and Manvantaras, of immense durations, should be looked at from this angle. Due to this inherent (self-imposed?) limitation, the Occidental scholars do not accept the historical existence of राम and just pass off the Rāmāyaṇa as a poetical work with mythical contents. From this, one should not jump to the conclusion that the Hindus have never paid any attention to history in their literary works and accounts. Both the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata—which are specifically termed as ‘itihāsas’ (‘thus, verily, did it occur’)—as also a number of पुराणस् have given enough astronomical data connected with all the important incidents narrated by them that it is possible to work upon them and extract the exact dates in terms of the Gregorian चलेन्दर्. According to one such attempt, the following are the dates specified for some of the incidents in the रामायण: 1 Birth of Rāma — 4439 B.C. His Banishment — 4414 B.C. His Coronation — 4400 B.C. Suffice it to say that the Hindu religio-cultural tradition has accorded the राम story a far greater reality, which does not preclude the historical aspect. 3. वाल्मीकि and His Work Maharṣi वाल्मीकि, the celebrated author of this great poem, the Rāmāyaṇa, is also one of the personages appearing in the राम story. He is one of the earliest sages whose hermitage राम visits in his sojourn through the forest after leaving अयोध्या. When राम banishes सीता, it is वाल्मीकि who shelters her and rears up her twin sons. Though the author, and a contemporary of the heroes in the Rāmāyaṇa, he gives pretty little information about himself. This is as it should be, since he was a sage who had dedicated his life to contemplation on God and service to humanity. He has revealed that he is a son of the sage Pracetas (sometimes identified with वरुण). लव and कुश, his disciples who sang the epic poem in the court of राम himself, introduced themselves as the pupils of भगवान् वाल्मीकि, a भार्गव (of the lineage of the sage भृगु). Piecing together the stories given in other works like the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, the Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa and the Bhāgavata this much can be said about him: He was a ब्राह्मण by birth belonging to the lineage of भृगु. Fate consigned him to a family of robbers which brought him up. Accidental contact with the सप्तर्षिस् (the Seven Sages) or with the sage नारद changed his life. By the repetition of Rāmanāma (the name of राम) he attain-ed the supreme state of a महर्षि or ‘great sage’. Since a valmīka or an anthill had grown over his body during his long period of austerities and since he emerged out of it when called, he came to be known as ‘Vālmīki’. The story of the origin of the Rāmāyaṇa is given in the epic itself, in the beginning. Once, नारद arrived at the hermitage of वाल्मीकि who received him with due honour and courtesies. Then he put a question to नारद enquiring whether there was anyone living at that time, embodying in himself sixteen great and noble qualities that go to make a perfect man. In reply नारद gave him the story of राम in brief. Then, immersed in the thought current of this story, वाल्मीकि left for the river Tamasā for his ablutions. There he witnessed the killing by a hunter of a male bird that was in love with its mate. The piteous wailing of the distressed female moved the heart of the sage so much that he spontaneously uttered a curse on the hunter. However, this curse came out of his mouth in the form of a ‘śloka,’ a perfectly metrical composition, which surprised the sage himself. When he returned to his hermitage, ब्रह्मा (the four-faced God, the Creator), appeared to him and commanded him to compose an epic poem on the story of राम as he had heard it from the great sage नारद, in this newly discovered metre. He also gave him the boon of the visions of all the incidents and the revelation of all the secrets connected with the story. Accordingly वाल्मीकि composed this epic, christened it as Rāmāyaṇa (‘The Way or the Conduct or The Life-story of राम’) and taught it to लव and कुश, the twin children of राम and सीता, through whom it gained vide currency and acclamation. 4. Date of the Composition If the Hindu traditional view is accepted, then the date of वाल्मीकि and his composition will be around 4400 B. C. राम's life are: Birth 4342 B.C.; मर्रिअगे with सीता 4327 B.C.; Exile 4315 B.C.; Return to अयोध्या and चोरोनतिओन् 4301 B.C. [D. S. Triveda, Indian Chronology, Bombay, भरतिय विद्य भवन्, 1963.]">2 However, the modern Western scholars and their Indian counterparts are wont to assign a much later period to this scripture, 400-200 B. C. Theories are also not wanting that try to trace the Rāmāyaṇa to the Daśaratha Jātaka of the Buddhists or identify राम with a Pharaoh of Egypt. They deserve to be ignored. 5. The Text The text as available to us now consists of 24,000 verses—24,253 to be exact—and is divided into seven kāṇḍas or Books. Each kāṇḍa is subdivided into sargas or chapters (total number of sargas being 647) and these comprise ślokas or verses. Though the work is almost entirely in the śloka or the anuṣṭubh metre, bigger metres like indravajrā or upendravajrā have also been employed. Three pāṭhas or recensions of the Rāmāyaṇa have been discovered so far: the Dākṣiṇātya (southern), the Gauḍīya (Beṅgālī) and the Vāyavya (north-western). There are some well-known commentaries in Sanskrit. They are: Tilaka or Rāmābhirāmī by Nāgoji Bhaṭṭa Śiromaṇi by Śivasahāya Bhūṣaṇa by Govindarāja Tattvadīpa, by Māheśvara Tīrtha Rāmānujīyavyākhyā, by Kandāla Rāmānuja Vivekatilaka by Varadarāja Dharmakūtavyākhyā by Tryambakarāja Rāmāyaṇa-kūṭa-vyākhyā by रामानन्द Tīrtha Most of these have been printed. Over the years, the रामायण scholars have struggled to discover which part of the text is the original and which is prakṣipta or the interpolated part. However, there has been no unanimity among them. Though the possibility of interpolations has to be conceded, it is not correct to say—as some opine—that the entire Uttarakāṇḍa is an interpolation. It is a genuine part of the original text. It may not be out of place to mention here that a ceremonial recitation of the text, especially during the रामनवमी (in April) and the Navarātri (during September-October) celebrations, is believed to confer great religious merit. 6. The Story in Brief BĀLAKĀṆḌA Daśaratha, the king of कोसल, was ruling from अयोध्या, the impregnable and matchless capital. An invincible warrior, a just and kind ruler, he had everything in life except worthy sons to succeed him to the throne in course of time. As per the advice of the sage वसिष्ठ, the royal priest, he performed the अश्वमेध sacri-fice followed by the पुत्रकामेष्टि rite, under the guidance of the well-known sage ऋष्यशृङ्ग. From the sacrificial fire there arose a divine being who delivered a vessel of pāyasa or pudding to दशरथ, instructing him to give it to his three queens—Kausalyā, सुमित्रा and Kaikeyī—so that they could bear him virtuous sons. In course of time कौसल्या, the chief queen, gave birth to राम, सुमित्रा to the twins लक्ष्मण and शत्रुघ्न, and, कैकेयी to भरत. Under the loving care of the parents and the watchful eyes of the preceptors, the children grew into boyhood. लक्ष्मण was very fond of राम and liked to be with him always. शत्रुघ्न was more attached to भरत. One day विश्वामित्र, the warrior turned sage, arrived at the court of दशरथ and asked for sending राम with him to protect his sacrifice against the depradations of the demons Mārīca and Subāhu. Hesitant at first, the king yielded and sent राम and लक्ष्मण with him. The two brothers successfully completed their assignment. And, in the company of that great sage, through his various journeys up to मिथिला, the capital city of the king जनक, they gained a vast knowledge of various subjects including the science of archery, of weapons and of war. At मिथिला, the capital of Videha, विश्वामित्र took राम and लक्ष्मण to the king जनक and requested him to show the Śivadhanus, the massive bow of Lord शिव, to the boys. Janaka had a daughter सीता, the paragon of feminine grace and virtues. He had declared that any prince or warrior who could string the Śivadhanus, would get her hand. Since a host of princes and warriors including the mighty ones had miserably failed to pass the test, जनक was a worried person. He now got it brought to the assembly hall and showed it to राम and लक्ष्मण. At the instance of विश्वामित्र, राम effortlessly lifted it up and tried to string it. In the process, unable to bear the pressure of his might, the bow broke into two with a thunderous noise. जनक and his family were extremely pleased. Daśaratha and his queens were summoned to मिथिला and the मर्रिअगे, not only of राम but also of the other three princes with suitable brides, was celebrated with due éclat. All of them returned to अयोध्या. On the way, राम vanquished परशुराम, the ruthless exterminator of the क्षत्त्रिय race who retired for penance. AYODHYĀKĀṆḌA After a few years, दशरथ, who was getting old, decided to anoint राम as the Yuvarāja (heir apparent) and retire. As the news got wind, the whole of अयोध्या went agog over it. कैकेयी, the third of the queens who had captivated the heart of दशरथ by her beauty, was incited by Mantharā, her crooked maid, to intercede with the king on behalf of her son भरत and demand the kingdom for him. Simultaneously, राम was to be banished to the forest for fourteen years. An unfulfilled boon given by दशरथ to कैकेयी, came in handy at this juncture and the physical absence of the noble prince Bharata—who was away at his uncle’s place—made things easy. Caught in a trap as it were, दशरथ had to helplessly acquiesce in. Rāma readily agreed to fulfil his ड़थेर्’s word. Along with सीता and लक्ष्मण, who importuned him to accompany him, he left for the forest. दशरथ, unable to bear the separation from राम, his dearest son, passed away in great agony. Meanwhile भरत and शत्रुघ्न were called back urgently by वसिष्ठ, the royal preceptor. After returning to अयोध्या and learning of the tragic events, भरत, nobility incarnate, railed against his मोथेर् कैकेयी, refused to accept the kingdom and started for the forest, vowing to bring back राम. When, at last, भरत succeeded in meeting राम at चित्रकूट in the forest and begged him to return, राम refused. Since it was equally incumbent on भरत to rule the kingdom for fourteen years, to fulfil the word given by दशरथ to कैकेयी, राम persuaded him to return to अयोध्या. भरत did so, taking the pādukās or the sandals of राम, which he coronated as the ‘King.’ He lived at Nandigrāma, a little village, away from अयोध्या, like a forest recluse, managing the affairs of the State as राम’s regent. ARAṆYAKĀṆḌA Now राम, along with सीता and लक्ष्मण, started moving in the forest going deeper, and farther towards the south, visiting the hermitages of many a great sage. Finally, after spending more than ten years, they settled down at पञ्चवटी in the दण्डक forest. One day शूर्पणखा, an ugly demoness with uglier intentions, came there. Captivated by राम’s matchless beauty she beseeched him to marry her. When राम and लक्ष्मण were having some fun at her expense, she tried to attack सीता. At this, लक्ष्मण cut off her nose and ears as a punishment, as per राम’s directions. She went to Khara, the demon chief, an overlord of this area of the forest and complained to him against राम. However, when Khara came and attacked राम with his huge army of 14,000 demons, राम, singlehanded, decimated them. The enraged and hapless, but vengeful, शूर्पणखा, approached रावण her brother and the king of लङ्का, to avenge her humiliation. However, knowing रावण’s weakness for women, she was wily enough to describe the bewitching beauty of सीता, the spouse of राम. Roused more by lust than by anger, रावण approached Mārīca, his erstwhile lieutenant and a past-master in cheating, to assist him in abducting सीता from the पञ्चवटी. Unable to dissuade रावण from his nefarious designs, Mārīca assumed the form of a golden deer, enticed सीता to hanker for it and beg राम to catch it for her. राम pursued it endlessly. Failing to capture it alive, he killed it. Mārīca, while dying uttered a loud cry, ‘Oh सीता! Oh लक्ष्मण!’ imitating the voice of राम. On hearing this, सीता, out of consternation, forced लक्ष्मण much against his will, to go to the rescue of राम. Finding her all alone, रावण abducted her and carried her away to लङ्का. जटायु, the giant vulture, a friend of राम, fought with रावण in vain to rescue सीता and became a martyr. Keeping her presence of मिन्द्, सीता while being abducted, dropped some of her ornaments among some monkeys perched on a mountain top. Rāvāṇa, after reaching लङ्का kept her captive in his pleasure garden, the अशोकवन. Rāma and लक्ष्मण returned to their hermitage, found सीता missing and started a vigorous search. In this process they encountered a demon कबन्ध and killed him (thereby redeeming him from a curse). Then they met शबरी, a woman-hermit of the forest tribe, accepted her होस्पितलित्य् and started towards the Ṛṣyamūka hill as per her advice with a view to meeting सुग्रीव, the vānara or monkey chieftain. KIṢKINDHĀKĀṆḌA Sugrīva, of the royal family of the kingdom of किष्किन्धा, was living on the Ṛṣyamūka hill, being banished by his elder brother वालि, who had also taken away his wife. राम forged friendship with him, killed वालि and restored the किष्किन्धा kingdom to सुग्रीव who was duly crowned. सुग्रीव promised to search for सीता and help राम to recover her. Later, सुग्रीव despatched his monkeys in all directions to find out the whereabouts of सीता. Since he and his able minister हनुमान् had seen a lady in distress in an aircraft, along with a monstrous figure, flying towards the south, he sent the more able of his troops to the south under the leadership of अङ्गद (Vāli’s son) and हनुमान्. This group arrived at the shore of the southern sea and started deliberating as to how to cross it. SUNDARAKĀṆḌA After some discussions among themselves, it was finally decided that हनुमान् should be deputed to go to लङ्का on behalf of them all. Accordingly he enlarged his body to massive proportions, using his special yogic powers, and crossed the ocean in one leap, overcoming all the obstacles on the way. After a thorough search, he found सीता in the अशोक grove, successfully talked to her, delivered to her the signet ring of राम, took her cūḍāmaṇi (crown jewel) to be given to राम as also her message, and returned to the other shore after doing immense havoc to the city of लङ्का and its ruler. When राम got all the news, he ordered सुग्रीव to mobilse his troops and march to the seashore. YUDDHAKĀṆḌA When the army was camping on the seashore, विभीषण, younger brother of रावण, alighted there from लङ्का and sought refuge at the feet of राम along with his four comrades. He had tried hard, but in vain, to prevail upon रावण to return सीता to राम and gain his friendship, thereby saving himself, his city and his subjects from utter disaster. रावण had not only spurned his sage advice but had positively humiliated him. Hence विभीषण, being a righteous person, had abandoned रावण and joined राम. After successfully building a bridge across the sea, the entire army of राम crossed over it, reaching the outskirts of लङ्का. राम’s final efforts at peace by trying to induce some sanity in the heart of रावण and get back सीता without war and bloodshed, failed due to रावण’s obstinacy. A terrific war ensued resulting in immense loss of life on both sides. There were periods of great tension and anxiety for राम and his army, as for instance when राम and लक्ष्मण were downed by the serpent missiles of इन्द्रजित् or when लक्ष्मण was struck unconscious by the शक्ति-missile of रावण. However, all such crises were overcome and all the dead in राम’s army were restored to life by the breeze of the Sañjīvanī mountain brought by हनुमान्. All the great warriors of रावण’s army including कुम्भकर्ण (the giant brother of रावण) and इन्द्रजित् (Rāvaṇa’s son) were slain. Finally रावण too was killed by राम thereby bringing the war to a close. Then राम put विभीषण on the throne of लङ्का and accepted सीता, after she underwent the fire-ordeal. By this time, fourteen years of banishment had been completed. All of them now returned to अयोध्या and met भरत and the queen-mothers. Rāma was then crowned as the king and सीता as the queen at a joyous and pompous ceremony. The reign of राम (Rāmarājya) was ideal in every sense of the term and all were extremely happy. It lasted for a long time. UTTARAKĀṆḌA Being overjoyed at the destruction of रावण and the establishment of राम-rājya, a number of sages, under the leadership of अगस्त्य arrived at राम’s palace. After राम duly honoured them, अगस्त्य narrated the stories of रावण and others in detail, just to make him understand how powerful and formidable they were. Then they returned to their hermitages. One day राम learnt from his spies about the rumours current in अयोध्या and elsewhere accusing him of impropriety in bringing back सीता to his होउसे even though she resided in रावण’s होउसे for quite some time. Shocked at this, राम decided to banish सीता to the forest and accordingly instructed लक्ष्मण to implement it. सीता, who was then pregnant, was given shelter by the sage वाल्मीकि whose hermitage was near the place where she had been abandoned. In course of time she gave birth to twins. They were named लव and कुश, and were brought up by the sage in a manner that befits princes. Some sages under the leadership of भार्गव and च्यवन came to राम and complained to him against the demon Lavaṇāsura. राम instructed शत्रुघ्न to go to Madhupurī, the capital city of Lavaṇa and destroy him. शत्रुघ्न accomplished the task easily and was crowned as the king there. He ruled for twelve years. Once the young son of a ब्राह्मण died and the ब्राह्मण blamed it on राम since it was an untimely death. Such deaths could take place only when there was अधर्म or unrighteousness in the kingdom. It was found out that a śūdra, Śambūka by name, was practising severe austerities, which was against the norms of that age. Hence राम was obliged to kill him. Years passed. राम decided to perform the अश्वमेध sacrifice in the Naimiśa forest. All arrangements were made. वाल्मीकि decided to attend the sacrifice along with his disciples including लव and कुश. They were instructed to sing the Rāmāyaṇa in all places of the sacrifice. They did so. Even राम heard it and was charmed by it. Later, when he learnt that they were his own children he sent word to Vākmīki that सीता should come to his court and reassert her purity. Though वाल्मीकि brought her and she did reassert her fidelity to राम she also prayed to मोथेर् Earth from whom she had emerged at the time of her supernatural birth, to take her away! The ground split into two and from it emerged भूदेवी (Mother Earth) with a throne. Seating सीता on that throne, by her side, she disappeared forever. The period of राम’s life on earth was fast coming to an end. So, the Kālapuruṣa (personified time) arrived at अयोध्या to remind राम that his play on earth was over and that it was time that he return to his abode. Due to the intrigue of the inexorable fate, राम was obliged to banish लक्ष्मण who was taken away by Devendra to हेअवेन्. After coronating his sons लव and कुश, राम retired to the सरयू river and then to his divine abode, after giving salvation to all the people of अयोध्या and others who had accompanied him to the banks of the सरयू river. 7. The Characters of the Rāmāyaṇa Before delving into the study of the various characters of the Rāmāyaṇa, especially of राम, one should carefully note the main purpose of the work itself. वाल्मीकि was a tapasvī, a holy man, who had practised severe austerities to realise the Truth within and to serve the society through the power of that realisation. It was not his intention to compose this epic poem nor was he a poet, competent enough to accomplish it. The simple question he put to नारद, the great sage, was to know out of curiosity, whether a perfect man existed then, who had in him all the great qualities that bespeak of a perfect being. He himself listed sixteen such qualities. If one did exist, he could as well become a model for the whole humanity to emulate. While admitting that it was difficult for a human being to possess even a fraction of these great qualities, नारद gladly confessed to the existence of such a remarkable man, राम by name, the king of अयोध्या, of the race of इक्ष्वाकु, who possessed these qualities in abundance and gave his story in brief. He even indicated the divinity of that personage. Brahmā, the Creator, chose वाल्मीकि as the instrument through whom the story of राम the perfect being, was to be widely disseminated, infilled him with the necessary power and commanded him to compose this great work. Hence, the Rāmāyaṇa that issued forth was a divinely ordained work, aimed at providing an ideal man to the world so that all the human beings could shape their own lives in his mould. Dharma is the keynote of this lyric poem. It is the basic principle that supports the whole universe. It expresses itself as conscience within and duties and obligations without. राम is its most complete representation so much so that he has become synonymous for धर्म for ages at a stretch. Other characters like लक्ष्मण, भरत or हनुमान् reflect different aspects of that धर्म in their life and doings, whereas रावण and his ilk exhibit the tragic consequences of its not being followed. Let us now deal briefly with these characters of the Rāmāyaṇa. RĀMA Rāma was extremely handsome. राम was extraordinarily strong. राम was par excellence, in the use of weapons and missiles, especially in archery which was his forte. Hence the use of the word ‘rāmabāṇa’ for any unfailing remedy in any field. He was a past-master in the science of war or the art of peace. He was deeply learned in the scriptural lore. His knowledge of literature or मुसिच् or लोगिच् was astounding. None could beat him in the finesse of conversation or consultation or negotiation. Yet, he was humble, affectionate and easily approachable. He rejoiced like a ड़थेर् in the happiness of his subjects and felt grieved at their sorrows and sufferings. Above all, he was deeply devoted to सत्य, truth. He spoke nothing but truth and, once word was given, he would keep it at all costs. He loved and served his parents. He was fond of his brothers, his wife and his friends. But, when it came to the protection of सत्य and धर्म, he would exercise his adamantine will and show that no sacrifice was too great to preserve these principles. To protect the truth of the word given by दशरथ to कैकेयी he gave up the kingdom in a trice and that too when he was about to be crowned! To protect the honour of his race and that of the crown and set an example in धर्म to his subjects, he subjected सीता, his dearest wife, first to the fire-ordeal and then, later, abandoned her even though he knew in his heart of hearts that she was pure and innocent! Daśaratha, who was a prisoner of his own making, urged राम to disobey him and even imprison him! भरत offered back the kingdom to him and earnestly importuned him to return. Even वसिष्ठ, the royal preceptor concurred with भरत! Notwithstanding all these pressures put on him by these beloved ones, राम not only refused to budge but also successfully convinced them of the correctness of his decision! When he returned to अयोध्या after duly completing the period of banishment, he did not hesitate to take back the kingdom and rule over it. However, he was even prepared to abdicate his right to the kingdom in favour of भरत, if भरत had by that time become attached to it. This only shows his extreme nobility and supreme indifference towards mundane comforts. While living in the forest, he adopted the way of life of the ṛṣis and munis (sages). And yet, as a क्षत्त्रिय warrior and an envoy of the ruler of the land, he did not forget his duty towards the helpless forest dwellers, especially when they beseeched him to protect them against the depradations of the राक्षसस् (demons). When सीता protested that he was misusing his might against the राक्षसस् who had done no harm to him, he unequivocally declared that it was his duty to chastise or even destroy the evil-doers who harmed the law-abiding citizens. He was prepared to abandon even सीता and लक्ष्मण, if need be, in the process, but not his धर्म! And this he did, when the need arose. In friendship also राम was absolutely loyal and steady. सुग्रीव sought his friendship. राम reciprocated. He killed वालि and got सुग्रीव crowned as the king of किष्किन्धा, thereby fulfilling his part of the covenant. But, सुग्रीव on his part faltered. On being pulled up by राम, he corrected himself and then plunged himself wholeheartedly in the service of राम. Now, a few words about the वालि episode that has raised a lot of hue and cry in the academic circles, accusing राम of अधर्म or unrighteous conduct. It should be remembered that the basic source of the whole story is the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि. In this work वाल्मीकि himself has solved the problem by showing that the very वालि who raised the objections first, accepted राम’s answer in toto and asked for forgiveness! Since वाल्मीकि did not create either वालि or राम but has only narrated whatever had happened between them, there is no need for anyone else, much less the persons of our gene-ration, removed as we are from them by a few millennia, to take up the cudgels on वालि’s behalf and run down राम! Suffice it to say that वालि knew better. Rāma was a great leader who knew the pulse of his followers very well. When विभीषण arrived in his camp and sought refuge, राम placed the problem before all of them and gave them full freedom to express their views fearlessly. Finally when he did take the decision, it was in perfect accord with his स्वधर्म, of not refusing shelter to anyone who sought it, even if it be रावण himself ! We should note that this decision of his was against the overwhelming—almost unanimous—decision of the war council he had called! Apart from his स्वधर्म, he had so much confidence in his own immense might that he was least afraid of even the mightiest of the enemies. Since he was sure of his victory over रावण and the conquest of लङ्का, he then and there got विभीषण crowned as the king of लङ्का, so that लङ्का and its innocent citizens would not suffer after the war. In the war with रावण and his army, राम always followed the path of rectitude even though the enemies often adopted unfair or even foul means and crooked strategies. Though he had to suffer in the process, he never wavered from it! During the very first combat with रावण, राम had worsted him so much that he could have easily killed him. However, his sense of धर्म was so strong that he permitted the enemy to escape from the battlefield with his life and limb intact, but also challenged him to come again after recouping for another round. When रावण was finally killed and when विभीषण refused to perform his last rites, राम admonished him and declared that he himself would undertake it if he did not! (Compare this with the present day war एथिच्स्!) Sītā was liberated. राम was happy. However, having known the psychology of the common masses who could crucify even a saint, he refused to accept her. The huge crowd comprising the vānaras and the राक्षसस् was watching with bated breath. सीता rose to the occasion. Her whole life was for राम’s sake. If he disowned her, she had no other alternative than death. To immolate herself in fire was her decision. राम did not object. He knew that her blazing purity would protect her from the fire. The fire that did not burn हनुमान्’s tail because of her command, how could it consume her at all? As expected, she was restored to राम unscathed. This was राम’s master-stroke that publicly proved the greatness of not only himself and his spouse, but also vindicated धर्म itself, that it protects those who protect it! Once राम assumed the reigns of the kingdom, he ruled it like a ड़थेर् and a मोथेर् rolled into one. Punishing the wicked, protecting the good and affording all opportunities to the subjects to lead a virtuous life was the hall-mark of his administration. Since he meticulously followed धर्म in his own life, even nature—which is also ruled by ṛta, the cosmic aspect of dharma—was kind to his country. However, even in the Rāmarājya—the country ruled by Rāma—there were people whose tongues wagged a little more than राम’s goodness and greatness could withstand. The central figure of this calumny was again the poor सीता! To protect the honour of the इक्ष्वाकु race and to keep his subjects within the limits of धर्म, the धर्म of family life, राम banished सीता to the forest where वाल्मीकि gave her shelter. सीता knew her lord’s compulsions and fully cooperated, never being bitter against him for this unkind act. The beheading of Śambūka, the sūdra ascetic, by राम has drawn the ire of many a critic of the Rāmāyaṇa story. A look at all the facts of the story and a dispassionate analysis of the same will reveal that राम acted in the best interest of the society and in accordance with the धर्म of the times. The शूद्रस् were not prohibited from performing तपस् or austerities provided it was for self-purification or self-realization. And, even for this they were expected to follow the injunctions of the śāstras (the scriptures honoured by the society) and śiṣṭācāra (conduct set up by the tradition of the good in the society). Śambūka was performing severe austerities with the intention of ascending to हेअवेन् in the human body! This was clearly against the scriptural injunctions and the norms for entry into हेअवेन् which required the acquisition of a divine and subtle body to fit in with the heavenly च्रेअतिओन्. It is obvious that Śambūka was very much attached to his physical body and—perhaps, against the wiser counsels of the wise ones of the society—was trying to force his entry as it were, into हेअवेन्. That means, the rules of the game had to be relaxed to cater to his whims, thereby disturbing the cosmic balance. It is akin to someone insisting on admission into the intensive care unit or the operation theatre of a hospital with his polluted clothes on, refusing to change over to the sterilized dress! If such a behaviour, that too if it is accompanied by an agitational approach, is condoned, the consequences would be catastrophic. The untimely death of the ब्राह्मण boy was only the first stirring of this since the subtle cosmic structure was getting loosened. Hence राम was right in doing what he did. If we remember राम’s affectionate treatment meted out to गुह and शबरी, who were also from the śūdra class, we can appreciate his conduct better. And, the revival of the dead boy back to life, confirms the rightness of राम’s conduct. Rāma was the personification of infinite compassion, love and consideration, and gratefulness. That is why when he ascended to his heavenly abode, he granted लिबेरतिओन् to all the citizens of अयोध्या who had accompanied him till the end. Whether राम was God become man or man become God, वाल्मीकि’s राम is intensely human. He loves, rejoices, weeps or gets angry or exhibits many other human moods like anyone of us. However, in and through all these, he has shown to what limits we can expand and evolve. That is why he has been called—and rightly so—‘Maryādā पुरुषोत्तम,’ the best of men who has expanded the human possibilities to infinite limits (maryādā = limit, border). The tribute paid by Mārīca, a demon and an erstwhile foe of राम, viz., that he was vigrahavān dharmaḥ (Personified धर्म), speaks volumes for राम’s greatness.
