LAKṢMAṆA If there is anyone in the Rāmāyaṇa who lived for राम and for nothing else or none else, it is लक्ष्मण. He was a paragon of loving service to राम. He was deeply attached to राम right from the childhood days. राम too was equally attached to him. Was लक्ष्मण irascible? Was he an agnostic who cared a fig for धर्म? Was he a disobedient and heartless son who despised his own ड़थेर्? Was he suspicious by nature? What were his achievements in life? Almost nothing? This description, this list of ‘vices,’ may appear to fit in well with लक्ष्मण as long as one does not understand the intensity or the depth of his love for राम. The one and only puruṣārtha or purpose of his life was to keep राम happy. Keeping that end in view, he was ever prepared for any service, any sacrifice, in his life. No one asked him to accompany राम to the forest. But he was ready even before राम was! He walked in front clearing the path. He built the huts for the comfortable living of राम and सीता. He gathered the articles of ड़ोओद् for them, cooked for them, served them and stood guard when they slept or rested. The hut he built at पञ्चवटी pleased राम so immensely that he saw in लक्ष्मण his own ड़थेर्’s love. When भरत came to the चित्रकूट with his huge army and retinue लक्ष्मण flew into a rage suspecting harm from him for राम. When he learnt of his noble intentions he was ashamed and melted in love. Rāma had hesitated to kill the demoness Tāṭakā since she was a woman and since killing a woman was considered to be a grave sin. But लक्ष्मण did not waver in the least to punish शूर्पणखा since राम had commanded him to do so. His duty was just to implement राम’s orders! Lakṣmaṇa was very intelligent and thoughtful. He could easily see through the māyā or the deceptions of the राक्षसस् behind the golden deer. He warned both सीता and राम about it. Unfortunately he did not succeed in preventing what actually happened. When सीता castigated him and threatened to commit सुइचिदे if he did not go to the rescue of राम (after the deer had been killed), he left with a heavy heart thinking that disobeying राम’s command was better than allowing the self-immolation of सीता. Yet, he could not escape the censure by राम! When राम was inconsolable due to the loss of सीता, it was लक्ष्मण who stood by him like a rock, often giving the healing touch by his mature advice and timely consolation. In the war with the राक्षसस्, लक्ष्मण fought bitterly not caring for his own life. His conquest of इन्द्रजित् was considered by the sages of the day, even more difficult of accomplishment than that of रावण by राम. His feelings, when he had to prepare the pyre for Sītā—during the fire ordeal—and be a mute witness to it, can better be imagined than described. When राम returned to अयोध्या and was coronated as the king, he offered लक्ष्मण the position of yuvarāja (heir apparent) which he flatly refused to accept since it would interfere with his service to राम! At the time of banishment of सीता it was again the poor लक्ष्मण that had to carry it out. It was worse than हेल्ल् for him. Just as राम was closeted with the Kālapuruṣa and लक्ष्मण was guarding the place with strict instructions not to allow anybody inside, दुर्वासस्, the sage known for his volcanic temper, appeared on the scene and insisted upon being admitted into the presence of राम. लक्ष्मण had only two alternatives before him: To admit him and face death as punishment at the hands of राम, or prevent him, thereby subjecting all to destruction by the wrath of the sage’s curse. लक्ष्मण made the supreme sacri-fice by choosing the former alternative since he did not want the entire अयोध्या to be annihilated. As soon as राम expelled him as a substitute for punishment with death, लक्ष्मण went straight to the सरयू river and gave up the body since there was no use living any more without his राम! BHARATA Though भरत was only next to राम in age, he conducted himself as the least of the brothers. If राम accepted the loss of the kingdom and expulsion to the forest stoically, भरत gave up the kingdom that was placed in his lap as his, since he could never accept the injustice done to राम. After severely reproaching his मोथेर् कैकेयी for all the havoc that had been wrought by her, he tried his best to bring back राम and coronate him as the king. When he did not succeed, he consented to rule as राम’s regent by installing his sandals on the throne and himself living in a village like a hermit, denying all the pleasures of life that had been denied to राम. Bharata had ruled the kingdom so efficiently that its properties and resources had been multiplied ten times. When राम returned, भरत offered the kingdom back to him immediately and felt greatly relieved. राम made him the yuvarāja. An ideal brother and an ideal devotee of राम, भरत continues to live in the hearts of Indians for ever. DAŚARATHA The picture of दशरथ that we get while reading the Rāmāyaṇa is that of an old man, a weak king, a lustful prisoner of कैकेयी’s beauty and a ड़थेर् doting on his son राम. However, in his younger days, he had proved to be a great warrior, capable of driving his रथ or chariot in daśa or ten directions—hence the name Daśaratha—and an able as well as popular ruler. His greatest defect was his impulsive nature, of giving promises without discretion or discrimination. It was this that made him promise अश्वपति Kekaya, ड़थेर् of कैकेयी, that her son would be crowned as the king. Again it was the same trait that made him promise विश्वामित्र to give whatever he wanted and then try to back out when he wanted राम to be sent with him. It was again the same story that repeated with कैकेयी, leading to untold misery and even his own death under tragic circumstances. SUGRĪVA किष्किन्धा were known as vānaras. Who exactly they were, will be discussed later. (See Page 88.)">3 On returning to अयोध्या after the exile, राम introduced सुग्रीव to भरत as their fifth brother. He fully deserved that remark and status by his surrender to राम and dedication to his cause. However, it took quite some time for him to rise to that level. Though सुग्रीव was himself a strong man and a great warrior, the repeated defeats and hammerings he had received at the hands of the powerful but vicious वालि had made him extremely suspicious, nervous and cowardly. That is why he suspected राम and लक्ष्मण at first sight as वालि’s spies. He gained full faith in राम’s prowess only after testing him in more than one way. He was intelligent, shrewd and worldly-wise. He was also addicted to the lower pleasures of life like sex and drinking. However, by the deft handling of राम he came round quickly and proved to be a great asset. After being crowned as the king of किष्किन्धा, सुग्रीव made arrangements to gather all the vānara warriors from different places at किष्किन्धा to help राम in his search for सीता. He then retired into his harem and forgot all about his responsibility as the king and his duty towards राम. When राम sent लक्ष्मण as his envoy to caution him and even warn him, सुग्रीव pacified the irate लक्ष्मण through तारा. Then he plunged into his task earnestly. Once the whereabouts of सीता were known, सुग्रीव mobilised his forces and marched towards लङ्का under the leadership of राम. The help he rendered to राम both personally and through his army of monkeys was invaluable. He even fought a duel with रावण on seeing him for the first time and returned after inflicting humiliation upon him. This being an impulsive and rash act, he was pulled up by राम. Rāvaṇa tried to entice सुग्रीव away from राम but got a severe rebuff. His loyalty to राम was, by now, absolutely firm. He fought bravely and killed many a rākṣasa warrior. His eagerness to witness राम’s चोरोनतिओन् made राम bring him and all the vānara heroes to अयोध्या. He was honoured suitably. When राम decided to leave for his heavenly abode, सुग्रीव also accompanied him. HANUMĀN Hanumān can be considered as the brightest jewel, a veritable diamond, in the necklace of Rāmāyaṇa characters. His physical strength and prowess were proverbial. His mastery over the scriptures was unmatched. His speech was not only faultless but also elegant. His intelligence and shrewdness were, by any standards, extraordinary. His common sense was uncanny. Even his facial appearance, though belonging to the race of the vānaras, was bright and pleasant. Above all, his devotion to राम was supreme, towering far above all other qualities. Anyone, as राम himself admits, who has such an one as his servant or envoy or minister, should deem himself as the luckiest of beings and there is no task that he cannot accomplish. Hanumān was the son of Añjanādevī, born as a result of the grace of Vāyudeva (the god of wind, also known as Marut). Hence the appellations आञ्जनेय and Māruti. The blow delivered by इन्द्र, by his वज्रायुध, on his jaw (= hanu) when he was a baby, to check his menacing prowess, left it swollen and hence he came to be known as ‘Hanumān,’ ‘one with a prominent jaw’. He was educated by no less a person than सूर्य, the Sun-god and acquired immunity from various weapons, as per the boons of the gods in हेअवेन्. Once as a child, he incurred the wrath of some sages by his michievous pranks that were too much to bear. They cursed him that he would not remember his strength until someone reminded him about it. This silenced him, preventing him from harassing the hapless sages. When सुग्रीव was driven out by वालि from किष्किन्धा, हनुमान् chose to leave the country along with him, even though वालि begged him to stay on, since he knew that धर्म was on सुग्रीव’s side. He voluntarily underwent all the hardships for सुग्रीव’s sake. When राम and लक्ष्मण arrived at the foot of the hill Ṛṣyamūka, सुग्रीव deputed him to find out who they were. His manner of approach—reverent and courteous—as well as his refined speech impressed राम so much that he gave vent to his admiration. Convinced of their nobility and greatness हनुमान् carried them to सुग्रीव and eulogised them before him. The attraction of हनुमान् for राम and राम’s special affection for him that sprouted on that first meeting grew to phenomenal proportions and have now become a legend. When वालि was killed by राम, and तारा, his queen, was inconsolable with grief, it was हनुमान् who succeeded in restoring her mental balance and peace by timely advice with an effective philosophical discourse. Again, when सुग्रीव had steeped himself in sensuous pleasures neglecting his duties of the State, it was हनुमान् who roused him out of that stupor and advised him to apologise to राम through लक्ष्मण. When सुग्रीव sent four batches of his troops in the four cardinal directions in search of सीता, he sent हनुमान् as a leader of the southern batch, since the possibility of finding सीता in the south were the brightest. Rāma too gave his signet ring to हनुमान् with the necessary instructions of what to communicate to सीता when found. This clearly shows the faith that they reposed in him. After reaching the southern shore of the land mass, the vānaras became despondent. अङ्गद, their leader, even spoke of staying back permanently! हनुमान् effectively intervened and through his wise counsels successfully prevented what might have resulted in a division of the country of किष्किन्धा. This shows his farsightedness and loyalty to the cause he had committed himself. Hanumān crossed the vast ocean with a mighty leap, overcoming all the obstacles on the way. He entered the city of लङ्का after vanquishing the demoness लङ्का the protectress of the fort-city. He searched for सीता in every nook and corner, especially in रावण’s palace and the harem but was disappointed. That the seeing of the women of the harem in various uncouth postures did not upset his steady मिन्द् in any way is a tribute to his ब्रह्मचर्य or celibate life. Realizing that such a पतिव्रता (a chaste lady deeply devoted only to her husband) like सीता could never consent to be in the palace of an abductor, he started searching for her elsewhere. Finally he found her in the अशोक grove, the pleasure garden of रावण behind his palace. Hanumān had to use all his wisdom and tact to establish contact with her and to develop a personal rapport. Once that was done, the rest was easy. He gave her राम’s signet ring and message, and, reassured her of राम rescuing her very soon. He took the cūḍāmaṇi (crestjewel) from her to be delivered to राम as also her message. Hanumān, though his task was fulfilled, did not want to leave, without leaving a mark, a warning shot as it were, to the enemy. So he contrived to meet रावण and also have a surveillant view of his city by destroying his favourite pleasure garden and killing all the rākṣasa warriors that came to capture him. Later, wilfully submitting himself to इन्द्रजित्’s ब्रह्मास्त्र, he succeeded in meeting रावण in the courtroom of his palace, admonished him severely and advised him to return सीता honourably to राम or be prepared to face decimation at his hands. Due to रावण’s wrath, when हनुमान्’s tail was set on fire by his aides, the vānara hero destroyed the city by that very fire. He then triumphantly returned to राम and सुग्रीव who immediately started on an invasion of लङ्का. सीता, लक्ष्मण & हनुमान्">Rāma with सीता, लक्ष्मण & HanumānDuring the war, हनुमान्’s heroic exploits were many. Even the mighty रावण could not stand the intensity of his blows! After the death of रावण at the hands of राम and the formal चोरोनतिओन् of विभीषण as the king of लङ्का, सीता had to be given the good tidings. This privilege was naturally conferred on हनुमान् who did it so successfully and gracefully that सीता was all praise for him. Out of his intensity of devotion to सीता and his sensitivity to her intolerable suffering under the rākṣasīs (demonesses) हनुमान् offered to punish them severely. The offer, however, was rejected outright by सीता, the compassionate मोथेर् of all. Along with विभीषण and सुग्रीव, हनुमान् also went to अयोध्या to attend the चोरोनतिओन् ceremony of राम. When the पुष्पक-विमान, the divine aircraft, alighted in the hermitage of the sage भरद्वाज, it was again हनुमान्’s prerogative to act as the messenger of राम to भरत, then living at नन्दि-grāma. In this he endeared himself to भरत almost instantaneously. After the चोरोनतिओन्, राम gave a priceless necklace to सीता giving her the freedom to grant it to anyone she deemed fit. Again, it was none other than हनुमान् who received the gift. Since हनुमान् decided to stay back in this world as long as राम’s legendary story was recited and listened to, राम blessed him before he left for his heavenly abode. Though coming from the किष्किन्धा culture, considered to be a little lower than that of अयोध्या, हनुमान् stands as the brightest example of human excellence. VIBHĪṢAṆA Vibhīṣaṇa is one of the dazzling gems not only among the राक्षसस् but also among the other votaries of राम. भीष्म and Droṇa of the Mahābhārata, though they knew that दुर्योधन was morally wrong in usurping the kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas, ultimately sided with him. True, they advised him and even admonished him. But, to them, obligation to a person became more important than commitment to धर्म! विदुर was a little better. He not only severely admonished दुर्योधन and his tribe but also stayed away from participating in the iniquitous war. But विभीषण of the Rāmāyaṇa made history by deserting the camp of the wicked and fighting against it from the camp of the good and the noble. No doubt he had an ambition for becoming the king of लङ्का as राम himself has admitted. But, coming from the royal race, he could not abdicate his claim to the throne and responsibility to the kingdom since it involved saving लङ्का ultimately, from ignominy. Being sāttvika by nature, goodness and devotion to धर्म were natural to him. Even when he practised severe austerities along with रावण and कुम्भकर्ण, and ब्रह्मा appeared before him to bless him, he asked only for his मिन्द् being firmly established in धर्म! ब्रह्मा, pleased with him, granted him the additional boon of being immortal even here. Śurpaṇakhā too and later on रावण himself, concede his righteousness and goodness. In रावण’s caucus of sycophants he was the first to boldly declare रावण’s abduction of सीता as utterly wrong and sinful and to exhort him in various ways to send her back to राम with all honour due to her and to राम. In this battle for righteousness he had many an encounter with रावण’s aids and even with इन्द्रजित्, his own young nephew. Yet, he successfully stuck to his guns and silenced them all. But for the utter humiliation and insult heaped upon him by रावण in his insolence, विभीषण might have continued to live in लङ्का, persevering in his efforts to bring back sanity into his behaviour. But that was not to be. When he finally decided to cross over to राम’s side, he never hesitated, since he knew in his heart of hearts, that राम would neither punish him nor desert him. His innate faith in राम’s greatness and nobility was his forte. The first thing that राम did was to symbolically crown him as the monarch of लङ्का. This automatically enhanced विभीषण’s faith in him. Since विभीषण’s surrender and राम’s acceptance were both complete and perfect, विभीषण spared no effort in helping राम to overcome all the obstacles created by the राक्षसस्, especially the ones centred in māyā or delusory powers. His help to राम, particularly during the beheading of the Māyā-सीता (illusory सीता) was timely and invaluable. After रावण’s death, विभीषण at first refused to perform the last rites for him. Being admonished by राम and realizing his duty, he completed it as per the dictates of the scriptures. The lifelong bonds of brotherly affection then made him break down with sorrow and lamentation. However, he quickly overcame the same and regained his usual composure. He too attended राम’s चोरोनतिओन् at अयोध्या, enjoying his loving होस्पितलित्य्. When राम finally departed from this world, he commanded विभीषण to return to his kingdom and rule over his subjects by धर्म. विभीषण was not allowed to open his mouth and protest, because लङ्का needed his benign rule! RĀVAṆA Even the strongest of chains breaks at its weakest link with little effort. Even the mightiest of men gets liquidated by his own mortal sins. रावण the ‘loka-रावण,’ who ‘shook the worlds’ once, is the supreme example of this eternal principle. He had great physical strength, was handsome and stately in appearance, possessed vast knowledge of the वेदस् and was an expert in the use of weapons and in waging wars. However, his uncontrollable lust, as also his arrogance, brought about his utter ruination. Endowed with natural strength and prowess, and boosted further by the boons he had secured from ब्रह्मा, the creator, he was a terror to the whole world. There was no warrior whom he had not vanquished or killed, no sage whom he had not humiliated, no woman whom he had not molested during his nefarious invasions and victory marches. He was shrewd enough to forge friendly ties with those who were a match to him so that his evil deeds could go on unhindered. Kārtavīrya and वालि belonged to this category. But neither mercury nor sin can be digested that easily! The tears of the chaste women and the anguished cries of the holy hermits along with their curses weighed heavily upon him, finally bringing him down. Sītā proved to be his nemesis. From the day she was brought to लङ्का, its fate was sealed. Odious omens started to appear in abundance foreboding evil to the whole society and its king. Not only विभीषण, even the trusted lieutenants of रावण, had noticed them with dismay and had warned him of the impending disaster if the remedial measure of returning सीता was not implemented immediately. But the die had been cast. Being a prisoner of inordinate lust and an aggressive ego, रावण could never get out of his self-created and self-nurtured predicament. He never hesitated to sacrifice the lives of his trusted generals, his near and dear relatives, even his own brother and sons, for bolstering his position. The very fact that he got कुम्भकर्ण woken up before the allotted period of six months, even though he knew well that, that would mean his sure death, is proof enough for this. In his fight against राम and his army, रावण employed every means, fair or foul, to defeat or destroy the enemies. When nothing worked and his own forces were steadily getting decimated, रावण realized that he was now paying through his nose, for all his sins and misdeeds. But it was too late. In desperation he even tried to behead the poor सीता, since she was ‘responsible’ for all his ills! Timely intervention by the saner elements around him saved her life. Rāvaṇa had been worsted in his battle against राम earlier, who had mercifully let him off the hook. But, when the final battle ensued, there was no escaping. He fought bravely and bitterly, but was brought down by the infallible missile (Brahmāstra) bearing the name of the very person who had endowed him with many boons and powers! Rāvaṇa stands today as the supreme example of the tragedy that can strike anyone who misuses and abuses his talents and powers, against the good and the noble, against the innocent and the holy. KUMBHAKARṆA Endowed with a mountainous body and an appetite of astronomical magnitude, कुम्भकर्ण possessed a simple heart and an intellect tempered with a sense of justice. When his very existence in the waking state—he used to eat up the living beings by scores at a time to satisfy his ravenous appetite—became a disaster for the world, the gods successfully worked out a stratagem with the assistance of सरस्वती (the goddess of speech) and the concurrence of ब्रह्मा, the Creator, to put him to sleep most of the time. He would wake up once, that too just for a day, after a sleeping bout of six months. This saved the lives of millions of beings and salvaged the honour of the Creator himself. Kumbhakarṇa was present in the second advisory council called by रावण. He boldly admonished him and even gave a discourse on the duties of a king! However, his own nature soon overtook this streak of wisdom in him and he promised रावण to ‘set right’ everything by his own prowess. He then went to sleep. Within nine days after this, tragedy after tragedy struck रावण and he lost a good number of his sons and generals. So, he was obliged to wake up Kumbha-कर्ण from his phenomenal sleep, even though he knew of its disastrous consequences, since rousing कुम्भकर्ण half way through his sleep would mean his certain death. This time also कुम्भकर्ण was amazingly frank and gave the same advice. रावण frowned upon him. Seeing that he was in no mood to listen to words of sanity and wisdom, कुम्भकर्ण confessed to having given that advice as a matter of duty but agreed to do his bidding. रावण, of course, commanded him to fight. Kumbhakarṇa landed on the battlefield like an avalanche and started destroying the vānaras by catching them and eating them up. He almost succeeded in capturing सुग्रीव but the latter managed to escape after successfully amputating his earlobes and nose bridge. As he was rushing towards राम, विभीषण accosted him. कुम्भकर्ण’s heart melted out of love and compassion for him and advised him to make himself scarce lest he might be killed. Kumbha-कर्ण however appreciated and approved विभीषण’s decision to join राम and blessed that the rākṣasa race be saved by him. Kumbhakarṇa was finally mowed down by the powerful arrows of राम. Verily, he strikes us more like a tragic hero. By siding with the unrighteous conduct of his elder brother, though out of brotherly love, he sacrificed himself. It was, however, in vain. VĀLI Vāli was the son of Ṛkṣarajas, born by the grace of इन्द्र. सुग्रीव was his younger brother. He was the king of किष्किन्धा. He was extremely strong and had even routed रावण once when he had dared to battle with him. Vāli had been blessed by इन्द्र with a golden necklace that would add not only grace but also strength to him. Though वालि and सुग्रीव lived together in peace and harmony with mutual love and affection, fate brought about a deep chasm between them which persisted primarily due to वालि’s intransigent and vengeful nature. Once वालि, accompanied by सुग्रीव, went in hot pursuit after a demon Māyāvi by name who had challenged him. When the enemy entered a cave, वालि kept सुग्रीव at the entrance as guard and went inside. He did not return even after a long time. When blood flowed out of the cave, and सुग्रीव heard the noises of the राक्षसस्, he apprehended that वालि might have died. To prevent them from escaping, सुग्रीव blocked the mouth of the cave with a boulder and returned to किष्किन्धा with great sorrow. The ministers crowned him as the king. Sometime later, वालि returned after killing Māyāvi and was furious to see सुग्रीव on the throne. Though सुग्रीव surrendered and explained what had happened—that it was a genuine case of misunderstanding—the suspicious and vindictive वालि ruthlessly drove him out. He also usurped Rumā, सुग्रीव’s wife, in spite of the pleadings and the sensible advice of तारा, his own queen. He thus incurred a great sin equivalent to incest, for which he had to pay with his life at the hands of राम. While accusing राम for having killed him in this manner he had said that he himself could have recovered सीता for him. राम who knew better, had chosen सुग्रीव as his ally rather than वालि, because the former was a dharmātma, a righteous person and the latter was not. वालि being lewd by nature and a committed friend of रावण, the consequences for राम would not have been very pleasant. Either due to राम’s greatness or due to a streak of goodness in वालि’s own personality, वालि realized his mistake, accepted राम’s explanation, asked for his forgiveness and died a peaceful death. SĪTĀ Sītā, the immaculate, the ideal of Indian womanhood for ages, was the adopted daughter of Sīradhvaja-जनक, ‘Janaka’ being the surname of the family. She was found by him in the ground while ploughing it, as a part of sacrificial rites. Hence she was also called Bhūmijā or the daughter of मोथेर् Earth. Keeping her divine origin in मिन्द्, जनक had pledged to give her in मर्रिअगे only to him who would string the Śivadhanus (the great bow of Lord शिव) that was in the possession of his family. Many a warrior-prince had tried his hand at it but none had succeeded. राम did. And, the मर्रिअगे was performed with due éclat. सीता lived happily with राम for quite a few years in अयोध्या. When राम gave up the kingdom, chose to retire to the forest, सीता automatically followed him. That was how she had been trained by her parents in her स्वधर्म. Sītā was an ideal match for राम whether in physical beauty or एदुचतिओन् and culture or wisdom or steady faithfulness. Though she was obedient and ever ready to serve him, she freely expressed her opinion—what she thought was right—when the occasion demanded. When राम gave word to the sages of दण्डक forest that he would destroy the demons of the forest, she protested gently saying that the demons had done him no harm and reminded him that he had come to the forest like a hermit! However, when राम replied to her objections she accepted the same gracefully. The appearance of the golden deer at पञ्चवटी was a turning point in her and in राम’s life. The extraordinary beauty of the golden deer was so enchanting that she fell a prey to it in spite of the timely warning given by the shrewd लक्ष्मण. Though राम too was carried away by its beauty, he was more eager to satisfy the desire of सीता who had sacrificed everything for his sake and had never asked for a thing. The consequences were of course disastrous. When सीता heard the distressed voice of ‘Mārīca-राम,’ she was so unnerved—as women under such situations do—that she goaded लक्ष्मण to go to राम’s rescue. But, लक्ष्मण the wise one, did not want to stir out, leaving her unprotected. Then she openly accused him of the vilest of intentions, and even threatened to commit सुइचिदे if he did not go! Poor लक्ष्मण chose the lesser evil and departed. All the same he did not escape from severe admonition by राम. When रावण appeared on the scene in the guise of a monk, she, in her innocence, treated him with all the respect due to a monk. When he made his intentions known and then abducted her, she was shocked. She then realized her fatal mistake and repented for having accused and taunted लक्ष्मण. But it was too late! While being carried away and when she noticed some persons sitting on a hill, she had the presence of मिन्द् to drop some of her ornaments amidst them. This, later on, helped राम and सुग्रीव to locate the abductor’s place. While in रावण’s captivity she lived a very austere life. She ruthlessly spurned all his advances and treated him like straw. She was bold enough to advise him on धर्म and forcefully suggest that she be returned to राम with due honour. She even threatened to burn him up by the very power of her chastity but held herself since she did not have राम’s permission, nor did she want राम’s prowess to go waste. Her मिन्द्, all the while, was dwelling on राम and राम alone. Once हनुमान् appeared on the scene and she got the news of राम, her spirits got buoyed up. Her refusal to go with हनुमान् back to राम, bespeaks volumes of her sense of honour and propriety. Her prayer to अग्नि, the fire-god, to protect हनुमान् when his tail had been set on fire, and her refusal to permit हनुमान् to punish the wicked rākṣasīs reveals her motherly love and compassion. After राम killed रावण and crowned विभीषण as the king of Laṇkā, सीता was brought to राम at his bidding. But when राम spoke very harshly and disparagingly, she gave a spirited reply and chose to die by entering into fire rather than suffer ignominy. No sooner did she enter the fire, than she was brought out unscathed, endowed with even greater beauty and grace, by अग्नि himself. After this fire-ordeal, when राम accepted her, her joy knew no bounds. Following the चोरोनतिओन् of राम she enjoyed peace and bliss. However, when राम banished her to the forest even though she was pregnant—being shaken by the insinuations of the people of Ayodhyā—she took it in its stride, appreciating राम’s standpoint and reaction. The sage वाल्मीकि who sheltered her and nurtured her children, was eager to reunite her with राम. However, राम’s insistence on her proving her purity once again in public, brought the curtain down on her life once for all. She gracefully chose to leave the world rather than face the humiliation of proving her innocence and purity, time and again. But, even in her final moments, her only concern was राम, her lord. KAUSALYĀ Vālmīki does not give any information about कौसल्या’s antecedents. Though she was the chief queen of दशरथ, he had ignored her, due to his infatuation with कैकेयी and the fear of incurring her wrath. Having been deprived of his love, she lived more like a recluse or a nun, sustaining herself on the meagre funds granted to her. She used to spend a substantial part of this on the maintenance of Vedic students in a part of her palace. She was often harassed by the servants and others of कैकेयी’s household. On hearing that राम would be coronated as Yuvarāja, she started ceremonial worship and giving gifts in a big way. When राम broke the tragic news, she was naturally affected like any मोथेर्. Her great disappointment made her speak very harsh words to दशरथ wounding him deeply. However, his remorse and pitiable remarks begging for pardon, made her retract and apologize. She even remonstrated with राम saying that as his मोथेर्, her command—‘Do not go to the forest!’—should get precedence over his ड़थेर्’s! When राम gave convincing reasons she accepted the same and cooperated. On the arrival of भरत who was eager to make amends for all the havoc perpetrated by his मोथेर्, she spoke harshly at first, wounding his tender heart further. But, when she discovered his magnanimity, she immediately responded and treated him with the same affection that she showered on राम. How she greeted राम, when he returned to अयोध्या, can better be guessed than described. She was a simple woman with a golden heart who suffered much in life but maintained her nobility and dignity throughout. SUMITRĀ Sumitrā, the second wife of दशरथ, was superior even to कौसल्या in her equanimity, nobility and recognition of the divinity of राम. She did not weep and wail when लक्ष्मण decided to accompany राम to the forest. On the other hand she profusely blessed him, advising him to treat राम and सीता as his parents दशरथ and सुमित्रा. If कौसल्या, even Sitā, found occasions to vent their bitterness against कैकेयी, it was सुमित्रा alone who never did it. She bore all the hardships and ignominies, created by कैकेयी’s jealousies, with stoic heroism. That is why दशरथ called her as ‘tapasvinī,’ a hermitess. She solidly stood by कौसल्या, giving solace and comfort by her timely advice. By her words and deeds, she stands out as a remarkable woman. KAIKEYĪ Kaikeyī presents herself to us as an enigmatic personality. However, piecing together all the information we can gather about her, we can solve the riddle to a great extent. She was the daughter of a woman—the queen of अश्वपति, of Kekaya kingdom—who had been banished by her husband for her ill-humored nature. She had inherited her मोथेर्’s temperament, who had not cared even for the life of her husband! If physical beauty had equipped कैकेयी with the power to ensnare दशरथ, her impetuous nature had made it worse. All the persons in the palace, as also वसिष्ठ the royal preceptor, सुमन्त्र the chief minister and Siddhārtha (another minister), knew it and had taken her to task severely on various occasions. Even भरत did not have many kind words to spare for her! Bharata and शत्रुघ्न seem to have lived with अश्वपति most of the time. This loss of the company of her dear son had, perhaps, been compensated by her by immersing herself in the pleasures of the palace and harassing her co-wives. One thing however was certain: She loved राम as she loved भरत and was all praise for his noble qualities. Whether she too had a better side in her personality or whether राम’s sterling qualities could penetrate even her irascibility is left to one’s discretion to judge. But for the Mantharā factor, her reaction on hearing the news of राम’s prospective चोरोनतिओन् might have been pleasant. It was Mantharā who stoked the fires of her innate jealousy towards कौसल्या, the chief queen, which ultimately developed into a conflagration resulting in all the havoc. Daśaratha loved her intensely. But his love and attachment for राम were even more intense. Had he not been trapped by his own words and the boons he had granted earlier, he might have dismissed her demands and even disowned her unceremoniously. All his entreaties and piteous lamentations had no effect on her. Any woman, and a favoured wife at that, would not have been that bad. Extremely harsh accusations or harsher invectives, even by सुमन्त्र and वसिष्ठ, fell on deaf ears. All that she did, was for her dear son भरत. But she had not, obviously, expected his adverse reactions. When भरत too joined the chorus of criticism against her and decided to bring back राम, she must have repented for her hasty actions. She was also one of the persons in the forefront, to greet and welcome राम, on his triumphant return. She is a good example of persons spoiled by indiscriminate pampering by the loved ones. ŚABARĪ Śabarī is the only character in the Rāmāyaṇa which is ‘small’ but ‘beautiful!’ She stands as the supreme example of a person attaining beatitude by devotion and surrender to the गुरु or spiritual preceptor. Her real name is not known. The word ‘Śabarī’ just indicates that she was a woman belonging to the śabara caste. Śabaras were a forest tribe, classed among the शूद्रस् and living by selling honey and fruits gathered in the forest. She had a गुरु, मतङ्ग by name. He was a very great person, a knower of धर्म, who had practised severe austerities. He was perhaps the same sage who had cursed वालि for his evil deeds. शबरी was living in his hermitage as per his command given at the time of his departure from this world. Having directed her to wait until राम and लक्ष्मण came there and then leave the world after worshiping them, he himself had cast off the body in his Vedic fire. She too did the same thing after honouring राम to her heart’s content. There is a popular (mistaken) notion that शबरी gave राम fruits after tasting them, thereby implying that she gave उच्छिष्ट (food or eatable soiled by one’s saliva) to him. There is absolutely no basis for this belief either in the Rāmāyaṇa or in the allied works. As per the descriptions given by वाल्मीकि, she knew the manners and etiquette (yathāvidhi) of honouring guests. राम’s questions posed to her touch upon her austerities only. Once the purpose of her long wait was over by meeting राम and worshipping his feet and honouring him by giving the fruits she had gathered, she expressed her blessedness and bliss. It should specially be noted that the caste factor never came in the way of her honouring राम or राम responding to her service or her attaining लिबेरतिओन्. TĀRĀ Tārā, the queen of वालि and the मोथेर् of अङ्गद, is the only woman character of किष्किन्धा about whom वाल्मीकि has given some details. She was the daughter of Suṣeṇa, a vānara hero. Tārā was very beautiful and was also very intelligent, a combination not always very common. She was also good in the art of talking wisely and logically, with proper regard to time, place, person and situation. When सुग्रीव challenged वालि a second time, तारा appealed to वालि, not only not to fight with him—since he had secured the friendship and protection of the extraordinarily powerful Rāma—but to bring him back and make him the Yuvarāja and live in peace with him. However, her sensible counsel was not relished by वालि as he was being driven by his inordinate hatred towards सुग्रीव and his own super-ego. When वालि was mortally wounded, she was inconsolably griefstricken. Words of advice by हनुमान् and of consolation by राम brought her back to normal state. When सुग्रीव took over किष्किन्धा as the new king, तारा also became his wife as per the custom prevalent among the vānaras. When an infuriated लक्ष्मण sent by राम entered सुग्रीव’s palace, it was again तारा who spoke very sweetly and pacified him. When राम was crowned as the king, तारा also attended the चोरोनतिओन् ceremony along with सुग्रीव and other vānara heroes as also their womenfolk. MANDODARĪ Mandodarī (also spelt as मण्डोदरी), the chief queen of रावण, was the daughter of मय, the śilpi or architect of the राक्षसस् and the most brilliant exponent of the science of architecture now known as Mayamata. She bore रावण a heroic son—Meghanāda or इन्द्रजित्. She was so beautiful and resembled सीता in so many ways that हनुमान् mistook her at first, when he saw her in रावण’s harem, for सीता herself. She knew the evil nature of रावण, and in all probability, had tried her best to bring him to better ways of life. Her lamentation at the death of रावण, over his dead body described in a long passage, brings out her character brilliantly. She could easily intuit that राम was none other than विष्णु and सीता was लक्ष्मी, his divine spouse. She regrets that रावण by his evil deeds such as destruction of the sacrifices of the ṛṣis, upsetting the wheel of धर्म, employing dubious methods in warfare and molesting numberless women of all classes brought about his own ruin since the consequences of sins can never be escaped. By her dignity and sagacity she stands out as a rare exception among the women of the rākṣasa race even as विभीषण does among the men of the same race. 8. Civilization and Culture as Depicted in the Rāmāyaṇa Civilization and culture need not, or, do not, always go together. Advancement of civilization does not necessarily contri-bute to a refinement of culture. Civilization makes our life here and now, more easy, more comfortable. But, culture inspires us to use the good things of life that civilization keeps in our hands, in the best interest of all and in a way that brings long-term benefits. Civilization can, like the weeds that grow along with the crops, contribute to profanity too. Culture, on the other hand, with its stress on the moral and ethical values, and a holistic approach to life, can not only tone down its evil effects, but also elevate it to more sublime levels. The Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि mirrors both these aspects of life. It presents us with three typical and distinct civilizations and cultures: those of अयोध्या, लङ्का and किष्किन्धा. The description of अयोध्या, first under दशरथ and later under राम gives us an idea of its advanced civilization and culture. The city was full of palatial buildings elegantly decorated. The roads were well laid-out, broad, and kept clean by periodical watering. There were strong and well-designed forts filled with all the articles essential for the guards and their assistants. Armed forces were ever kept in combat-readiness. They contained many heroes who were experts in the use of weapons, especially in archery. However, they were magnanimous in battles and followed the rules of धर्मयुद्ध, like not attacking an unarmed enemy or one fleeing from the battlefield. People led a happy, peaceful and contented life. Study and propagation of the वेदस् as also the performance of sacrifices went on unhindered. The king administered the country very efficiently, ably assisted by the ministers, advisors, and sages who acted as royal priests. सत्य and धर्म (truth and righteousness) were the basic principles upon which the whole edifice of the State rested. The duties of the four varṇas and the four āśramas were scrupulously kept up and were also enforced if and when necessary. दशरथ being bound by the word he had given to कैकेयी, राम’s immediate compliance by renouncing the throne and going to the forest, सीता and लक्ष्मण following him of their own accord, भरत’s exemplary behaviour in trying to bring back राम, वसिष्ठ’s ever watchful eye in protecting the interests of the kingdom and its subjects—all these bespeak of a highly cultured society. Laṅkā under रावण was a very rich and prosperous city of dazzling splendour. But almost all its riches were the result of robbery or booty plundered in wars. The city abound in palaces and huge buildings, as also gardens. The citizens were physically giants with fierce appearance and ruthless behaviour. drinking as also cannibalism was quite common. There were also yāgaśālās (sacrificial sheds), but the ब्राह्मणस् were devoted to magical rites and sorcerous rituals. The temples were mostly dedicated to certain fierce deities like Bhadrakālī. रावण and इन्द्रजित् were wont to worship this deity at a secret place called Nikumbhilā, before a war, to acquire supernormal powers and weapons. Hence they were experts in māyāyuddha, wars using the magical powers of इल्लुसिओन् to deceive the enemies. Enjoyment of sensual pleasures was the main concern of the people. The city of किष्किन्धा has been described as a guhā or a cave. It was probably situated within a mountain range, the passage to which lay through a cave. The city itself was quite spacious, well-designed and beautiful, provided with all the necessities for a comfortable life, revealing an advanced civilization. Vālmīki has described the denizens of किष्किन्धा as ‘vānaras’ or monkeys with all the characteristic features of the monkeys or apes throughout the work. If we analyze the various facts provided in the epic, we have to come to the inevitable conclusion that the word is to be taken, not literally, but symbolically. The word ‘vā-नर’ may mean ‘or, perhaps, he is a human being’. The facial features of these vānaras might have approached those of apes by the rather prominent lower jaws. Since they spoke a human language and since the women had no tails and have been described like other women of the human species, we can conclude that the vānaras were also human beings but accustomed to live in the hilly regions, forests and banks of rivers. Maybe, they painted themselves like apes and wore a dress leaving a part of it at their backs or loins like tail. Maybe, the ape was their national symbol. They were physically very strong and used their own teeth and nails or implements of stone or branches of trees while fighting. They were, obviously, not used to warfare with artificial weapons, though they were experts in wrestling. The wearing of the यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) and performance of the सन्ध्या ritual was current among them. However, rules of मर्रिअगे and the regulation of man-woman relationship do not seem to have been governed by the higher ethical codes as in the अयोध्या culture. drinking seems to have been quite common, even among women. The level of their civilization was perhaps midway between those of अयोध्या and लङ्का. Laṅkā was rich and prosperous. रावण was a mighty king. He had learning and power. He could even practise severe austerities if and when needed. But his inordinate concupiscence and intense selfishness ruined him, destroyed his kingdom and almost decimated his subjects. Vibhīṣaṇa the lone crusader for धर्म, managed to save of लङ्का what little he could, by joining राम. But for him there would have been no लङ्का. Kiṣkindhā of वालि would have met with the same fate but for राम’s intervention brought about by the surrender of सुग्रीव to him. सुग्रीव’s sense of धर्म, however feeble it might have been in the beginning, and his devotion and dedication to राम, saved it from disaster. Ayodhyā under the noble इक्ष्वाकु princes, buttressed further by राम’s personality and example, rose to glorious heights, making it a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे for ages. This, then, is the philosophy of the Rāmāyaṇa: Wealth and power cannot save either an individual or a nation. It is devotion to सत्य and धर्म, character, that saves, that protects! 9. Rāmarājya—the Ideal State Rāma’s rule was so ideal that the word ‘Rāmarājya’ has now become synonymous with an ideal kingdom or an ideal State. We can get a fairly accurate description of an ideal State by putting together the three accounts given in the Rāmāyaṇa: a narration of दशरथ’s rule, the questions posed by राम to भरत at चित्रकूट to find out how he was ruling and the graphic description of Rāmarājya itself. Since the ‘Rāmarājya’ hinges on the ‘Rāma’ (the king) who rules, he should be an ideal person deeply devoted to the practice of सत्य and धर्म in his personal and social life. He should be ever vigilant in the welfare of the State. He must have a small group of ministers and advisors of proven character and competence. He should employ persons in jobs suitable to their temperament and capacity. There should also be a well-organised espionage system, preferably of three tiers. The ruler should disburse salaries on time and honour the heroes learned in the martial arts. He should confer rewards or mete out punishment to persons in proportion to their acts of commendation or blame. People having faith in God and the value-system based on the holy books should be protected and supported at all costs. Atheists and agnostics who cared not for this, should be put down with an iron hand. He should rule in such a way that the income is always in excess of expenditure. All those engaged in the production and proper distribution of wealth—the agriculturists, the traders, the dairy farmers and other persons in similar vocations—must be meticulously taken care of. More than everything else, it was the supremely sacred duty of the king to maintain the socio-ethical balance by protecting the वर्ण-आश्रम-धर्म of the subjects, punishing the transgressors severely when necessary. Since राम was an ideal man and an ideal king, his rule also was ideal. When he was ruling, people lived happily to a ripe old-age, without the fear of diseases or dacoits, wild animals or poisonous reptiles. All were devoted to धर्म and led a contented and peaceful life sans greed and sans violence since they could always see राम the ideal person before them, to emulate. Even nature was gracious unto them by giving them timely rains conducive to the good growth of crops and vegetation. 10. Literary grace If Hindu religious tradition treats the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि as a स्मृति (a secondary scripture next only to the वेदस्), the literary tradition accords it the title ‘ādikāvya’ (primeval classic) and calls वाल्मीकि himself as the ‘ādikavi’, the patriarch of poets. The work richly deserves this epithet and has been a model to be emulated by the later poets of the classical age. Vālmīki’s genius lies in his masterly use of the similes and metaphors. Whether it is the human sentiments of love and attachment, hatred and detestation, valour and fearlessness or the beauties of nature as the descriptions of the seasons or even the comical featuring of grotesque figures, his similes are always most apt and can conjure up the objects very well. 11. रामायण Literature The influence of the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि has been so powerful and deep that quite a few other Rāmāyaṇas have come into existence in course of time, thereby enriching our Rāmāyaṇa literature. Of these, mention must be made of the अध्यात्म Rāmāyaṇa (4200 verses) considered to be a part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. Modern scholars however feel that it is an independent work of an unknown author and assign it to the 14th century. Cast in the form of a dialogue between शिव and पार्वती, this work is highly devotional and is dedicated to the spreading of the cult of राम. It abounds in beautiful hymns and quite a few philosophical discourses including the well-known Rāmagītā. The Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa (12,000 verses), also called Manohara-आनन्द-Rāmāyaṇa is another popular work. It is also in the form of a dialogue, first between पार्वती and शिव and later between रामदास and his disciple Viṣṇudāsa. This work contains a number of stories popular even now, such as those of गोकर्ण, the famous पिल्ग्रिमगे centre in Karnataka and of the rākṣasa brothers Ahirāvaṇa and Mahirāvaṇa of the nether world who tried to help रावण. This work also is assigned to the 14th century or even a later date. Then there are some other Rāmā-yaṇas, also in Sanskrit, like the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa (1355 verses) the Yogavāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa (32,000 verses), the Tattva-saṅgraha Rāmāyaṇa and the Saṅgraha Rāmāyaṇa which have been printed but have not become popular except in limited circles. Quite a few पुराणस् also contain the story of Rāmāyaṇa, though briefly. Some minor उपनिषद्स् like the Rāmapūrva-tāpanīya, Rāmottaratāpanīya and the Rāmarahasya deal with राम as Parama-पुरुष, the Supreme Person himself. As regards the Sanskrit literary works based on the Rāmāyaṇa themes, they are legion. Other Indian languages also have been enriched by the Rāmāyaṇas based on वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa or its adaptations. The Rāmacaritamānasa of Tulasīdās (in Hindi), the Rāmāyaṇa of Kamba (in Tamil), the Ramāyaṇa of Kṛttivāsa (in Bengali), the Rāmacaritam and the Kannassa Rāmāyaṇam of Ceramān and Kannassa (in Malayalam), the Rāmāvatār of गुरु Govind Singh (in Punjabi), the Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇa (in Telugu), the Rāmacaritra of Girdhar (in Gujarāti), the Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa of Sarala Dās (in Oriya), the Rāmāyaṇa of Mādhava Kandali (in Assamese), the Torave Rāmāyaṇa of Narahari (in Kannada) are some of the more well-known Rāmāyaṇas in the vernaculars. 12. Rāmāyaṇas outside India The story of राम, either in its original form as depicted by वाल्मीकि or in a metamorphosed form, has travelled widely outside India, to Tibet and Eastern Turkestan, to South East Asian countries, Japan and even Mongolia. The following list of works—by no means exhaustive—gives an idea of this movement: Rāmāyaṇa Kakawin (Javanese) Hikayat Seri Rāma (Malaysian) Rāmakien (Thai) Pha Lak Pha Lam and Khvay Thuaraphi (Laos) Hobutsushu (Japanese) Rāmāśvamedha (Nepali) Jānakīharaṇa (Sinhalese) 13. Conclusion If the worth of a literary composition has to be judged by the effect it has had on a whole generation, the Rāmāyaṇa of Ādikavi वाल्मीकि stands out as supreme since it has influenced and is continuing to do so even now, generation after generation. Its tremendous impact on our religion, social values, literature, मुसिच्, drama, dance, painting and sculpture—in fact, on all aspects of our life—is very palpable. It has given us an ideal man who stood for सत्य and धर्म come what may. It has given us an ideal woman, the paragon of feminine grace and virtues. It has shown us an ideal family system where everyone thought of the welfare of everyone else first. It has given us the models of ideal brothers, ideal friends and ideal servants who spared no effort to bring comfort to the loved ones. It has put before us an ideal State. In other words, it has placed before us enough ideas and ideals to inspire us, to rise from the human level to divine heights. If this spirit is imbibed, a study of this scripture will be immensely profitable.

Ramaṇa महर्षि was, undoubtedly, one of the greatest spiritual giants of Modern India.
He was born at Tiruccuḷi in Tamil Nadu on the 30th December 1879 as the second son of Sundaram Iyer and Aḷagammāḷ. His original name was Veṇkaṭarāma.
One day in 1895, he accidentally heard the name of a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे dedicated to Śiva—Aruṇācala—which produced an ecstatic experience. Next year, he had another strange experience, as if he had died and was yet living, fully conscious, looking at his own ‘dead body’. This produced a deep conviction in him that he was the spirit transcending the body and the मिन्द्, generally called ‘ātman’ in Vedānta.
Soon after this experience, he left his home for good and went to Aruṇācala, in quest of that spiritual experience, to make it a permanent asset of his life.
There was a cave-like structure below the large temple hall, known as पाताल-लिङ्ग. The young mendicant started living there, mostly in deep meditation. During this period and later, some good Samaritans took care of him. He also had to change his dwelling place a number of times. His मोथेर् Aḷagammāḷ who tried to take him back home, ultimately started staying with him permanently.
Some of the places where he stayed before settling down at the present place (in A.

)—now known as Ramaṇāśrama—are: the Virūpākṣa Cave (17 years) and the Skandāśrama (6 years), both in the vicinity of the present आश्रम.
As his name—as an ātmajñāni (self-realised सोउल्) or a jīvanmukta, fully liberated person—spread far and wide, devotees, spiritual aspirants and others started pouring in, in large numbers. Tiruvaṇṇāmali (the town) and the Ramaṇāśrama, his abode, became a veritable place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Some of the prominent persons who were deeply influenced by him were: Kāvyakaṇṭha गणपति मुनि (a great scholar); Paul Brunton; Major A. W. Chadwick; S. S. Cohen and Arthur Osborne.
Brunton and Osborne have written biographies of the sage.
First signs of cancer (sarcoma) appeared on his left elbow in A.

. In spite of repeated operations, radium therapy and various other kinds of treatment, it did not subside. He passed away on the 14th April 1950.
The true nature of an ātmajñāni (a man who has realised his Self) was revealed in his life and personality, constantly and continuously. Silent radiation of intense peace was the chief characte-ristic of his personality.
His main teaching or advice to the aspirants was to find out “Who am I’ (Nān yār?). By a constant enquiry and self-analysis one arrives at the truth that he is the pure आत्मन् (of the nature of sat-cit-आनन्द, existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss) transcending the body-मिन्द् complex.
His most famous work is Uḷḷadu Nārpadu in Tamil. Its Sanskrit version is Sad-darśana by गणपति मुनि.
Another work, a spontaneous outpouring of marital love (or bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्) towards Aruṇācala शिव is Śrī Aruṇācala Akṣaramaṇa Mālai containing 108 verses in Tamil and composed during one of the circumambulations of the Aruṇācala hill.
There are also a few other compositions in verses containing high Advaitic sentiments.
There is no doubt that he was the brightest spiritual star of the most recent period, in the firmament of Hindu religion and philosophy.

Rāmagītā
(‘the song of राम)
------------------------------------------
Unlike the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa pictures राम not only as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of Mahāviṣṇu himself but also as a perfect spiritual preceptor.
The teachings given by him to his younger brother लक्ष्मण are found in three places: Araṇyakāṇḍa 4.19-55; Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa 4.11-40; and Uttara-kāṇḍa

.
However, it is the third discourse that is normally considered as the Rāmagītā.
It is full of the usual teachings on the Advaita Vedānta as propounded by शङ्कर (A.

-820) and his followers.
The following are some of the topics dealt with:
Lakṣmaṇa’s surrender to राम and his request for spiritual wisdom by which he can cross over transmigratory existence; need to purify one’s मिन्द् by the performance of one’s duties as per the वर्ण and the आश्रम; अज्ञान being the root cause of bondage, it has to be eliminated only by ज्ञान (or आत्मज्ञान); defects accruing to Vedic rituals; hence, the need to renounce कर्म or actions altogether; to get ज्ञान one has to approach a competent गुरु and get the teaching of a mahāvākya like tat tvam asi by applying the principle of bhāga-लक्षणा or jahadajahal-लक्षणा (See LAKṢAṆĀ for details.); description of three kinds of śarīras; आत्मन् is free from all kinds of changes; on अध्यास or super-imposition; different schools of Advaita Vedānta; methods of निदिध्यासन or meditation on the आत्मन् leading to its realisation; how to associate the three syllables of the प्रणव or Om with this meditation; the inevitability of prārabdha कर्म; final dissolution into the आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन्; राम is ब्रह्मन्.
There is another Rāmagītā consisting of about a thousand verses spread over eighteen chapters in a less-known work called Gurujñāna-vāsiṣṭhatattva-sārāyaṇa which deals with the subject in a slightly different way. It also deals with sixteen विद्यास् or modes of upāsanā (like the ones in the उपनिषद्स्), चक्रस् or yogic centres in the body as also सिद्धिस् or miraculous powers of the yogins. Many practical aspects of sādhanas are also dealt with.

Rāmanavamī
------------------------------------------
Eight days after युगादि or on the ninth day of the bright half of the month of चैत्र, falls the birthday of Śrī राम, one of the two most popular and highly revered incarnations of Lord विष्णु. He is said to have been born at noon.
The Rāmanavamīvrata is नित्य or compulsory for the devotees of राम and optional for others. One of the highly eulogized vratas in the Hindu चलेन्दर्, it can destroy one’s sins and also confer even मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
Actually the vrata commences from the previous night itself with ड़स्तिन्ग्. On the navamī day also the votary has to continue ड़स्तिन्ग्, perform worship and होम to राम in an image installed in a specially prepared shrine, do जप of Rāmamantra and keep vigil in the night. After the completion of the vrata he has to donate the image to the आचार्य (a learned ब्राह्मण well-versed in the rite) along with other gifts made liberally.
In the modern days gifting the image of राम is extremely rare. ड़स्तिन्ग् is done by the more orthodox persons only. However, people do assemble in very large numbers in राम temples and enthusiastically participate in the festivities there. Pārāyaṇa or ceremonial recitation of the Rāmāyaṇa (usually spread over the nine days from युगादि), arranging religio-cultural programmes like हरिकथा (musical discourse on mythological stories) and classical मुसिच् or devotional songs are quite common.
Celebrations at places associated with राम, like अयोध्या in Uttar Pradesh and रामेश्वरम् in Tamil Nadu attract thousands of devotees.

If the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि has made the story and the personality of राम immortal, the Rāmacaritamānasa of तुलसीदास (A.

In other parts of North India, the same is celebrated as the victory of the good over the evil, by burning the effigies of रावण, कुम्भकर्ण and मेघनाद (or इन्द्रजित्).

Rāmarahasya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
A minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda, the Rāmarahasya Upaniṣad has 157 verses spread over five chapters. The third chapter is completely in prose. Other chapters too contain prose passages here and there. It is in the form of a long dialogue between the sages led by सनक and devotees like प्रह्लाद, with हनुमान्, the matchless devotee of राम.
The speciality of this Upaniṣad is that it deals with several esoteric mantras of राम, their uses, yantras (mystical diagrams) and rituals.
A brief account of the same may now be attempted here.
First chapter (15 verses)
Sanaka and other sages along with the devotees of Lord विष्णु, like प्रह्लाद and विभीषण, approach हनुमान् and ask him what the tattva or the ultimate Truth is.
Hanumān replies that राम is the highest Truth, the ब्रह्मन् that helps one to be saved from transmigratory existence.
He further states that himself, गणपति, सरस्वती, दुर्गा, क्षेत्रपाल, सूर्य, चन्द्र, नारायण, Nārasiṁha, वायु, Vārāha as also सीता, लक्ष्मण, शत्रुघ्न, भरत, विभीषण, सुग्रीव, अङ्गद and जाम्बवान् are the aṅgas or limbs as it were, of राम. Their mantras (esoteric formulae) should be repeated first to get the grace of राम.
He next deals with the efficacy of Rāmamantra of six letters as also the simple Rāmamantra of two letters with प्रणव (Om) on both sides.
This is followed by विभीषण’s question to राम himself about the method of destruction of heinous sins. राम replies that by repeating ‘Rāma’ 96 crores of times, it is achieved!
If one is unable to do this, the same result can be attained by repeating daily any one of the following: This Upaniṣad, Gītā, Rāmasahasranāma, Rāmāṣṭottara-śatanāma, the hymns composed by नारद or हनुमान्, the Sītāstava and the six lettered मन्त्र of राम.
Second Chapter (106 verses)
This is a veritable mine of mantras. on राम starting with one letter, up to 31 letters. This is then followed by an anuṣṭubh मन्त्र (32 letters), a गायत्री मन्त्र (25 letters) and a mālāmantra (a very long one, of 48 letters). Mantras of सीता, लक्ष्मण, भरत, शत्रुघ्न and हनुमान् are also given.
Some of the mantras may now be given as a sample: rām; राम; Oṁ राम; śrīṁ śrīṁ yaṁ namaḥ; rāṁ rāmāya स्वाहा; rāmacandrāya namaḥ; Oṁ rāmāya huṁ phaṭ स्वाहा; Om namo bhagavate rāmacandrāya; Om namo bhagavate rāmāya sakalāpannivāraṇāya स्वाहा; klīm Oṁ namo bhagavate rāmacandrāya sakalajanavaśyakarāya स्वाहा and so on.
The Rāmagāyatrī is: dāśarathāya vidmahe, sītāvallabhāya dhīmahi, tanno rāmaḥ pracodayāt.
The other mantras are: śrīṁ sītāyai स्वाहा; laṁ lakṣmaṇāya namaḥ; bhaṁ bharatāya namaḥ; śaṁ śatrughnāya namaḥ and haṁ hanūmate namaḥ.
The other formalities (purificatory processes) connected with these mantras such as nyāsas, ṛṣi (sage), छन्दस् (metre), ध्यान ślokas (verses describing the forms of the deity) are also given at the appropriate places.
Third Chapter (4 paras, all in prose)
This short chapter deals with the yantras or esoteric geometrical diagrams of the various mantras and their worship.
Fourth Chapter (13 verses)
This section describes the rules of पुरश्चरण (details connected with the repetition of the मन्त्र, in a systematic manner) of the various mantras.
(See TANTRAS.)
Fifth Chapter (19 verses)
The बीजाक्षर (seed-mantra—rāṁ) is described as a combination of ब्रह्मन् and Māyā. It is the seed from which this ‘tree’ of the world has evolved.
The two-lettered word ‘Rāma’ can give भोग (enjoyments here) or मोक्ष (liberation) as per the aspirant’s desire since it contains in itself the meaning of the famous Vedāntic dictum tat tvam asi, ‘that thou art’.
The Upaniṣad concludes with the eulogy of the Rāmamantra which can give fruits of all kinds, including मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Those who study this Upaniṣad, will become so pure that they are untouched by even heinous sins, but become one with राम Himself.
